Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition such as $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, $\phi$ must be equivalent to the successor function, defined as incrementing a number by 1. Finally, we explore a more complex generalization of this result, substituting the earlier operator assumption with a more complex condition.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. Nonetheless, these models are inadequate to learn optimal user and item representations. Collaborative filtering methods, including user-based and item-based, due to their efficiency and clarity, have long been utilized in building recommender systems by generating profiles for each user and item based on their historically interacted items and users. Our research integrates these methods with context-aware document models by taking into account users' perspectives on these items. Additionally, our model offers the advantage of online personalization where the system can adjust the user and item representation profiles upon detecting new user interactions without requiring updates to the model's parameters. Our proposed algorithm was tested and demonstrated superior performance on three real-world datasets when compared to baseline methods.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that freeness of type $B$ is equivalent to conditioned freeness of type $C$. We extend known freeness results to include mixed circular unitarily invariant random matrices. By comparing freeness with other, related matrix convexity properties, we analyze the tensor and free cumulants of unitarily invariant random matrices and discuss their implications in statistical physics and quantum chaos. Notably, we explore the functional relations between empirical spectral distributions, distribution of eigenvalues, and eigenvalue density. We examine the distinct scenarios in which these quantities do not remain fixed as $N$ increases. Additionally, we derive the asymptotic distance between adjacent eigenvalues of randomly rotated matrices within the same spectral segment. We investigate the mode and median of the Wigner distribution

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and on the mixing between $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ resonances, both of which are known to be heavily produced. Our analysis suggests that the primary contribution comes from processes involving the $\rho$ meson. This leads to the observation that the ratio of branching ratios for these decays is essentially the same as the corresponding ratio for $\bar B^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ and is therefore expected to be near 2. Furthermore, our results for the latter process are such that its error bars are small enough that the experimental and theoretical results for this process are now roughly equivalent.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a) a pupil tracker captures images of reference lasers using a $2 \times 2$ lenslet array, while b) a field tracker captures images of the science target; c) a pupil imager re-images the telescope's pupil, and d) an aberration tracker captures images of a Shack-Hartmann sensor. The camera's detector images are analyzed using dedicated software to determine beam stabilization parameters, every 0.7 seconds. The obtained parameters are then applied to a) adjust the GRAVITY instrument to align with VLTI; b) actively stabilize the telescope's pupil and field of view; c) perform defocus correction, as well as various engineering tasks. The camera has successfully transitioned into operational use, with data reduction and on-sky characterization results having been documented.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced doubling and highway dimension complexity. Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue and shows how it yields an efficient scheme with specific parameters when dealing with supplier networks of limited highway dimension and limited doubling dimension, but not with networks characterized by highway dimension. This highlights a distinction in how these dimensions behave, establishing the Capsacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers issue as the first known example illustrating such a distinction.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system as well as the error rate. As part of an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors, we build on earlier studies, including [VoulisJedrzejowiczLyon2021], which provided a minimum threshold for evaluations in terms of field complexity, with a proof based on an information-theoretic argument. In this study, we develop a proof that the same threshold is achievable, with a concrete evaluation scheme that uses fewer computations than [GarciaTriggs2014] when error rates are high. Additionally, we introduce an innovative technique called "early termination" that allows us to stop evaluations mid-process once enough information has been obtained to solve the system, offering a new metric for measuring the required number of evaluations beyond field complexity.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a combination of single and multi-photon emissions, and can be achieved using isolated driving fields or multiple driving fields with carefully chosen frequencies. The protection afforded by parity symmetry remains effective for both static and time-varying couplings between the cavity and the driving fields.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - a fraction that can be arbitrarily close to 50% - without exceeding a linear bound on the number of messages, delivering an accurate estimate within a linear margin of the true value. Additionally, when the fraction of malicious nodes does not exceed 25%, the algorithm provides a tight bound on the estimated value, inclusive of a linear margin. Furthermore, the algorithm uses a single universal constant as its error bound, avoids dependency on the network's diameter, and provides no information that could be used to localize the malicious nodes.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse Traceless equations to include non-conforming regions with vanishing conformal trace. By introducing a new parameter, $\alpha_0$, that governs the stability of the solution in terms of the L2-norm, we are able to construct a well-posed solution to the Hamiltonian constraint. This new method performs comparably to the standard method but allows for a greater range of values for $\alpha$ and is less sensitive to grid effects. Additionally, with $\alpha_0$ set to a high value, the approach can be extended to cover regions with arbitrary (finite) curvature in the Hamiltonian constraint. However, this leads to solutions with higher error values. Furthermore, the approach is capable of handling initial data with varying levels of curvature and mass distribution, including fixed mesh and adaptive grid scenarios.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment is to closely observe the Mei beta decay by means of large-scale neutrino observatories. To achieve this goal, the collaboration has been developing 20-inch low-power photomultiplier tubes with a high quantum efficiency of 350nm. In order to meet these requirements, the experiment's PMTs needed to be tested for their dark rate, including the impact of thermal energy, using specialized equipment. The research involved constructing a thermal chamber with temperature control capabilities, allowing the investigation of the dark current at various temperatures ranging from 40 to 70°C. The study's results showed that the number of dark events increased by one occurrence every 230,000 seconds for every degree of temperature rise. Furthermore, the research highlighted the significance of monitoring the PMT's temperature in real-time as it directly affects the readout system's gain.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent work employing the Informer model based on the Transformer architecture has yielded impressive results for long-term forecasting, yet it falls short in addressing dimensional interactions. Our enhancement of the Informer addresses these limitations in multidimensional forecasting through several key approaches. Firstly, we incorporate an adaptive graph neural network module to capture dimensional cross-interactions, and secondly, we tailor the adaptive graph structure according to forecasting error across different dimensions, thus optimizing its full potential. Our empirical evaluations on diverse datasets showcase that the proposed framework achieves exceptional forecasting accuracy and modeling efficiency compared to the baseline Informer model and alternative methods.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a better position to inform the development of improved ADCs for the future, and advise against relying on the Zemax model, especially when blue spectrum accuracy is critical.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted inference performance in large-scale labeling tasks, such as semantic segmentation. To achieve this improvement, model distillation from multiple experts into a single student model, utilizing unlabeled data, is usually employed. However, when applying this technique to labeled tasks, it is hindered by the constraint of having access to labeled data during the training process of the student model. To resolve this limitation, we propose a new approach called Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), which allows for multi-expert labeled distillation using only pair-wise labeled data. PILE iteratively combines logits from the teachers and learns to correct it via supervision from the student's ground truth. Our experiments show that PILE, even when applied to models with low cardinality, achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence compared to conventional knowledge distillation methods on CIFAR10 and ImageNet datasets. Additionally, PILE demonstrates the ability to handle a larger number of teachers and provides more robust performance even when dealing with noisy teachers.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency, because low-frequency fluctuations will occur as well due to its wave-like properties. A detector can therefore look for these low-frequency fluctuations, rather than just its high frequency oscillations, and is not limited to finding frequencies that are easily within its range, but can actually be searching for much larger and unexplored ranges of frequencies. A network of sensors, by cross-correlating their measurements, can detect these low-frequency fluctuations, and is not limited by bandwidth because low-frequency fluctuations will occur simultaneously at a range of frequencies. In this way, existing sensor networks can be used to experimentally explore the unexplored ranges of the parameter space of this bosonic dark matter.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of the BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of the solution rely on the eigenvalues of this matrix being distinct or real, which holds for most choices of the Haar measure. The properties of the solution set are complemented by a stability estimate that dictates the accuracy of the solution's approximation for any given approximation of the problem's data. The theoretical findings are confirmed by numerical experiments.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing heuristic-based mapping algorithms to optimize P416 programs for different hardware resources. This allows rapid prototyping of different mapping approaches and provides resource usage metrics for comparison.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. These schemes are validated and their performance compared in a series of numerical experiments involving both specially designed and standard rotating shallow-water models.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in a way that ensures accuracy and facilitates a comprehensive mathematical analysis. Our experiments with a computer vision task utilizing CIFAR-10 data sets reveal that the combination of fairness metrics and differential privacy, when applied simultaneously with federated learning, yields higher test accuracy compared to implementing them sequentially.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify new excited states of a specific subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart, largely due to a lack of understanding the effects of conservation and dissipation. In this research, a model that exhibits non-intuitive scattering behavior is analyzed, featuring a compact, three-dimensional hyperboloid with a chaotic Poincare map. By integrating numerical and theoretical approaches, the impact of conservation and dissipation on the system's phase space and basins of attraction is studied, revealing that weak dissipation significantly influences the system's dynamics and enhances the formation of Wada basins. The findings indicate that a particular dissipation value optimizes the system's ability to form Wada basins, with implications for the design of complex systems and their inherent characteristics.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (neutral) quark currents is considered, where the transition of this scalar into hadronic quark matter is explored through a parameter $c_H$ and further constrained by low-energy hadronic quark data. In addition, we analyze the interactions between this scalar with charged lepton pairs $(\ell^\pm \ell^\pm)$ and di-muon pairs, which can be significantly produced at $e^+ e^-$ colliders such as LHCb, muon factories and in dark matter indirect detection experiments using muon decays. This is made possible by the fact that the desired interaction combinations are not prohibited under the standard model, and our study serves as an extension to existing SM pressure and quark gluon coupling constraints. We have found that the scalar's durability can be prolonged up to $10^{17}$ seconds, and further speculate that its lifespan could potentially exceed that of the universe itself. This theoretical model also raises questions and suggests new areas of research within the SM, and could be explored using various experimental facilities to a considerable extent.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance superiority.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, when this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a near-extremal black hole with a different mass, but with a smaller charge.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three entropy estimation methods derived from this framework are introduced, tested, and validated on simple and more intricate scenarios, including a case study involving a neural network's output distribution.

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation focuses on the existence and distinctness of solutions with specific initial conditions. We demonstrate that various types of initial data can yield both unique and multi-fidelity solutions. Notably, when the underlying space is one-dimensional and a particular fidelity is chosen, the model's solutions exhibit a form of differentiability. In addition, we have found cases where the common assumption of non-decreasing velocities fails, which has implications for the original model's interpretation as a flow. These findings highlight the need for further clarification of the model's physical meaning.

Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices with IoT or industrial applications. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool that effectively combines noisy data removal and efficient data encoding, leveraging the benefits of Naive Bayes classifier while reducing resource requirements. In this study, three NBcoded implementations are developed using three Naive Bayes likelihood distribution assumptions (Gaussian, Complement, and Bernoulli). By comparing the results, NBcoded shows exceptional performance in training time and disk usage efficiency while only slightly underperforming state-of-the-art classifiers, such as Multilayer Perceptron and Random Forest, with a relatively minor reduction of 2% in accuracy and F1-score.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its implications on G's set actions. We then explore Schreier growth gaps for solvable groups. If G is metabelian and finitely presented or torsion-free, but not virtually abelian, it possesses a Schreier growth gap of n^2. If metabelian G has a Krull dimension of k, it will have a Schreier growth gap of n^k, such as the Schreier growth gap n^d for the wreath product C_p ∋¬ ℤ^d and n^(d+1) for ℤ ∋¬ ℤ^d. For solvable groups of finite Prüfer rank, a Schreier growth gap of exp(n) applies unless they are virtually nilpotent, a criterion which also applies to solvable groups linear over ℚ. Lastly, a wide range of torsion-free solvable groups have a Schreier growth gap of n^2, a group type that also includes those linear over ℚ.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw visual data collected over time. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical temporal patterns in different directions, distinct from human-induced motion that often lacks these asymmetrical time patterns. A species, when moving forward, typically displays temporal symmetry in image sections along the direction of the movement, whereas, when moving sideways or backward, the patterns become asymmetrical. This document presents seven distinct categories of biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to detect biolocomotion, forward movement, sideways movement, and the difference in movement speeds in any given direction. A dataset comprising videos of vertebrates and vertebrate larvae, along with turtles, finned creatures, and flying creatures has been used to evaluate our proposed approach, showing significant results compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights the significance of discrepancy models in data-driven physical inference and illustrates a method for automatically generating these discrepancy models using ML techniques. The simulation results confirm the accuracy of the proposed discrepancy model in simulating the falling motions of objects without prior knowledge of their physical properties. Furthermore, this work shows that physical parameters can be estimated using ML techniques from measurement data, and such estimates are found to be less prone to error than those obtained through traditional force analysis. Finally, this work proposes a new definition for a perfect physical law that incorporates both experimental data and theoretical predictions.

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower speeds than light and distinctive characteristics: substantial transverse momentum and unusually large energy loss per unit length. The study focuses on particles detectable by their tracks in the inner detector and energy loss measurements in the pixel layers of the detector, thus able to capture particles with lifetimes as short as one nanosecond and masses ranging from 100 GeV to 3 TeV. The study explores the possibilities of long-lived particles in supersymmetric models, considering the production of $R$-hadrons, charginos and staus, with mass limits that extend well beyond previous search findings in various scenarios.

We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the finite element method. A design optimized for a 1D nanobeam cavity yielded a notable source efficiency of 97.7 percent and an impressive Purcell factor of 38.6 for an isotropic dipole, primarily due to a combination of high index contrast between GaAs and SiO$_2$ materials and an effective cavity design that facilitated interference and minimized losses. However, we also identified mode mismatch as a limitation of our platform and suggested enhancements such as incorporating an air gap in the system to improve single-photon source efficiency and overall performance.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved, thereby facilitating the calculation of dynamic structure factor and sound wave proportions within and below the boson peak, a technique which has been applied to various substances like silicon dioxide, boron oxide, polybutadiene and amorphous germanium. Studies on temperature-dependent boson peaks in silicon dioxide and glycerol have also been conducted. Furthermore, x-ray Brillouin scattering measurements have demonstrated that longitudinal sound wave damping in silicon dioxide and glycerol follows a soft potential model prediction, $\omega^4$, particularly in the low-frequency regime.

Feynman integrals are increasingly complex calculations that confront theoretical physics. The growing demand for precise calculations in particle physics and condensed matter is driving the need for advanced analytical methods. This review highlights recent breakthroughs in evaluating complex Feynman integrals, specifically those involving multi-loop and large/massless/massive scale combinations. The review offers solutions to a range of integral families that are of common occurrence in physics evaluations, along with discussion of future applications in physics and potential evolution of Feynman integral analysis.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be followed in a map of Galactic longitude and velocity as a faint feature extending at least 20 degrees. Both the far-side and near-side arms exhibit comparable features including velocities, widths, heights, and mass distribution. Based on further investigation using 21-cm data, it's found that these spiral arms are primarily composed of molecular gas. This new evidence lends support to the presence of a bar structure at the center of the Galaxy and should aid in understanding its properties.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. However, in the absence of design, obtaining a broad range of solutions can be challenging. We offer several design methods grounded in recent research, intended to facilitate the integration of phenotypic diversity within optimization processes.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable valuations and three-dimensional groupings, was explored, revealing instances where no stable matches exist and a direct approach for finding one in polynomial time, by reducing it to a convex programming problem, along with proving that such instances can be resolved within a 40-fold improvement in efficiency compared to existing solutions. Additionally, we investigated the challenges of finding stable matches for situations with potentially negative values and showed that such instances can be resolved within a 4-fold improvement in efficiency compared to existing solutions. Finally, we proved that finding stable matches for situations with potentially negative values in general cannot be resolved within a linearly improved efficiency compared to existing solutions.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When we restrict
our study to constant strain conditions, we observe that two mechanisms, cone tilt
and deformation potential, yield analogous effects on valley Hall and valley
polarization cycles. However, this equivalence does not hold when we account for the
dynamic behavior of the strain. Our findings indicate that the valley Hall effect
peaks at a specific chemical potential and that the valley polarization is
proportional to the square of the difference between the chemical potential and
the Fermi level. Our study also shows that the valley polarization can be controlled
by adjusting the doping level in the system.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. To explain this phenomenon, we investigated the stability of these space transformations. This paper demonstrates that any cloud having a stabilizer with nontrivial action will contain a unique central metric space, such that transformations from the stabilizer all converge to this space, thereby indicating that it is zero distance away from all others within that group. The key proof for this lies within our previously established cloud completeness theorem.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for each resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth. The input impedance and the wide beamwidth were closely examined through simulations and comprehensive analyzed with the aid of the far-field pattern and surface current distribution. The measured outcomes showed an operational stability over temperature ranging from -20 to 60 degrees Celsius.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. The approach is shown to exceed the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability and practicality.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that hadrons traveling in the same direction as high-energy photons exhibit lower yields in Au$+$Au collisions compared to $d$$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons moving opposite to the photon's direction show little variation in yield across these three sets of collisions. These results suggest that hadrons may be suppressed in the presence of a high-energy environment and a medium that interacts with quarks and gluons. This suppression may offer insight into how these particles lose energy to the medium.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. This relatively straightforward connectivity arrangement makes the digital-analog method particularly appealing for fermionic quantum simulations.

A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias towards handling OoD scenarios.

This robust feature set is generated using the Rich Feature Construction (RFC) algorithm, inspired by Support Vector Machines, which produces a high-dimensional feature space that encompasses both in-distribution and OoD data points. The algorithm is adaptable to various scenarios, such as open-set, semi-open-set, and semi-supervised out-of-distribution domains. The richness of the features is independent of the model's parameters and can be calculated independently. This property makes RFC versatile and efficient to implement, outperforming alternative methods in multiple scenarios.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness approach, design an innovative iterative, real-time hybrid system, and incorporate an active detector system all tailored for forming intricate patterns despite the inherent complexities in tissue and other scattering media. By utilizing our proposed methods on a 3D tissue phantom with embedded fluorophore, we've demonstrated the formation of multiple fluorescence-emitting structures, including a two-dimensional spiral pattern, and an overall distribution of fluorescent light that can be optimized for future applications in opto-acoustics or other treatment therapies.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we distinguish our research from Kallus (2020) in Section 1 by highlighting their distinct assumptions, variations, and research objectives. In Section 2, guided by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020), we analyze the efficient policy evaluation problem using data from both the training and testing distributions. Our results demonstrate that under specific growth conditions, efficient value function estimates can yield strong performance, although connections with the existing literature reveal limitations under slower testing sample size growth. In contrast, the testing sample size requirement for DRITR is more relaxed than that of efficient policy evaluation using combined data. In Section 3, we emphasize the broad applicability and utility of DRITR.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, a small collection-electrode monolithic demonstrator. Particle beams are utilized to analyze the charge collection properties and device performance across different thicknesses under various beam angles. In CMOS sensors utilizing a high-resistivity substrate, a notable enhancement is observed, with the sensitive volume increasing two-fold, significantly benefiting monolithic tracking systems.

Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Even with advanced technologies like adaptive optics, there are certain limitations that prevent us from achieving this goal. Specifically, speckles in space, caused by atmospheric distortion, pose a major issue. While current wavefront sensors can detect and adjust for some of these speckles, they often fail to effectively manage the system's noise, ultimately limiting our abilities. A new technique known as the fast atmospheric self-coherent camera, or FAST, offers an effective way to effectively manage and eliminate these speckles at high speeds. Tested on the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics testbed, the FAST system successfully demonstrated the ability to effectively manage and eliminate speckles at speeds of 200, 400, and 800 Hz, with the ability to detect and adjust for speckles even when they are not visible to the human eye. This breakthrough technology will play a critical role in allowing us to reach the levels of performance needed for the next generation of telescopes.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and accurately replicating the observed yield curve. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, incorporating the deterministic-shift adjustment. For quick alignment with the current swaption prices, the Gram-Charlier expansion is employed to calculate swaption prices within the proposed framework. Multiple numerical evaluations, utilizing Monte-Carlo simulations, demonstrate the precision of the Gram-Charlier approximation, often matching the four-point moment expansion error.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the design of DUNE's Near Detector, so we calculated the anticipated sterile neutrino decays within the detector's volume. According to our projections, DUNE may establish a limit comparable to past predictions made for LBNE. We visualize these results for each neutrino type – electron, muon, and tau – indicating that DUNE has a promising capacity to explore previously unexplored areas of sterile neutrino parameter space before the SHiP experiment joins similar research initiatives from CERN and other institutions.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators is essential to accurately assess the precision of their meta-regression estimates.  This research extends the application of such estimators to the bivariate meta-regression analysis, enabling the simultaneous examination of two effect sizes and their relationship.  A comprehensive simulation study compares the performance of three cluster-robust estimators: the standard, damped, and unbiased variants.  The simulation findings suggest that the weighted, damped, and unbiased variants exhibit similar performance in the bivariate meta-regression context, highlighting the efficiency of the weighted approach.  When applied to real-world data sets, the application of the weighted, unbiased variant yields plausible results.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while producing similar outcomes.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained via numerical analysis are then compared with LHCb and ALICE experimental findings for nuclear broadening in the context of J/Psi particles. Notably, models that align with small-x data are shown to yield transverse momentum variations consistent with measured values, especially in cases where rapidity is in the forward direction. Additionally, model consistency with ALICE measurements is found across various centrality levels.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: $a^2+ab+b^2 \equiv 1 \mod 7^n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency for HPC applications in systems using non-volatile memory, with a focus on minimizing performance overhead. This method involves detecting crashes, directly using the properties of algorithms, and then implementing a simple and efficient recovery mechanism that allows the application to continue running without interrupting the computation. Our approach is characterized by low overhead, particularly during normal operation, and can be easily integrated into existing compilers without requiring modifications to the source code. Experimental results demonstrate that this method yields substantial performance improvements over current state-of-the-art checkpointing techniques, allowing HPC applications to achieve high levels of crash consistency with only a minor increase in overhead. For instance, the _md5_ application can achieve this with only a 1.42% performance penalty, while other applications such as _swim_ and _bbq_ accomplish the same feat with even lower penalties of just 0.14% and 0.67%, respectively.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful themes from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the predicted absorption as a function of binary energy and angular momentum, and the distribution of lifetimes. Our results showed that escape probabilities matched theoretical predictions with high precision, marking a significant improvement over previous statistical theories. Furthermore, the measured values of the exponent near marginally unbound escape thresholds agreed well with an independent, flux-based prediction. Both findings support the flux-based three-body statistical framework, and our measurements of absorptivity and lifetime distributions provide valuable resources for further testing and validation of statistical models.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, at an extent comparable to that found in previous 2.76 TeV collisions. The study also found that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons does not vary by rapidity but decreases slightly at high transverse momentum levels above 25 GeV/$c$ when compared to lower momentum levels. The findings suggest that the suppression of these charmonium states at high transverse momentum is due to their formation by the combination of quarks and anti-quarks that have been altered by the medium.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, alterations to its structure can have unintended consequences, hindering performance and causing the system to crash. This research addresses the challenge of identifying test cases for a software system to ensure its reliability after a structural change. We've developed an algorithm using singular value decomposition to determine suitable test cases, and our findings demonstrate its efficacy on real-world data, even in the presence of noise. Additionally, we've refined this algorithm for parallel processing on multiple CPU cores, significantly boosting its speed for large-scale datasets.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate that the incorporation of Ecological Momentary Assessment records significantly increases the recall of the model in predicting suicidal ideation, from 48.13% using Electronic Health Record data alone to 67.78%. Furthermore, the proposed method offers enhanced interpretability through dimensionality reduction in the latent space and medical feature analysis.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a range of 3-6 keV originating from Cassiopeia A with the help of the IXPE. Following the analysis of a 291 ks exposure, a map of X-ray polarization was created by combining the most polarized directions of two identical telescopes, resulting in an average polarization of $(1.8 \pm 0.4) %$ with a related error. Our findings indicate that the reverse shock wave has a prominent role in generating X-ray emission and associated polarization, supported by observational data and theoretical models, which show good alignment between the predicted and observed polarization maps. Furthermore, our data reveal individual radiation directions from radioactive isotopes $^{44}$Sc and $^{56}$Ti within the supernova remnant with notable significance, displaying average polarizations of $(4.0 \pm 1.1 ) %$ and $(3.1 \pm 1.3 ) %$ in the 3-4 keV and 4-5 keV ranges respectively. These findings provide the first direct evidence of polarized X-rays emitted by $^{44}$Sc and $^{56}$Ti, which is consistent with predicted emission patterns, thus validating the theoretical models.

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of $a_n$.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are driven by diffusion, surface phenomena such as wetting and drying lead to highly complex and dense networks of interfaces. The interfaces formed exhibit self-similar patterns of fractals, where local interface structures repeat at higher resolution. The overall behavior of the system is influenced by its spatial distribution; thus, analyzing the topology of these interfaces requires a combination of quantitative metrics and representation methods. This study introduces a new approach for characterizing the topology of dense multiphase systems through a technique called skeletonization, which decomposes the interface into simple, geometric representations of its major features. A novel skeletonization method, inspired by medical imaging techniques, is introduced and applied to gas-liquid systems, resulting in a set of relevant topological metrics. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated on various microscopically observed dry foam samples.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be an example of viral surface metabolism, where the collection of spike proteins interacts with the carbohydrates, generating mechanical movement through a self-organizing process. This research aims to investigate in greater detail the physical aspects underlying this rolling motion, developing a theory that explains the motor's behavior, as well as validating the results using simulations to analyze the impact of various factors. The outcomes of this study strongly indicate that viral movement on surfaces is statistically certain to occur when the virus exhibits enzymatic activity.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be a significant mechanism contributing to U galaxy warping.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic structures called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The arrangement of atoms within these crystals permits the existence of chirally behaving phonons, which correspond to atoms circling their equilibrium positions. Given that inversion symmetry and time reversal symmetry govern the total pseudo-angular momentum of the system, this momentum is zero. By introducing dopants, researchers find that this can result in a new crystal structure, F$\bar{4}3$m. Novel materials, KRbBi$_{4}$ and RbCsBi$_{4}$, exhibit no dynamic instability; the inversion symmetry disruption however, leads to phonons with a non-zero total pseudo-angular momentum. Chirally behaving phonons emerge at wave vectors located at the Brillouin zone boundary in both systems under consideration. By exploring this possibility of phonon engineering through doping, researchers open the door for further investigation into the phonon Hall effect and identify two potential materials for further analysis.

In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how the positioning of individual atomic sublattices generates electric polarization, a concept seemingly unrelated to metals and doped semiconductors. However, our findings reveal that, when the conventional approximation is surpassed, nonadiabatic Born effective charges become well defined in metals within a specific frequency range. We also observe that, unlike in insulators, the summation of nonadiabatic Born effective charges from sublattices in metals does not equal zero but rather correlates directly with the Drude weight. These conclusions were verified through calculations using density functional perturbation theory, as applied to aluminum, and to two doped compounds, electron-doped tin disulfide and strontium titanate.

We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, although many people have ignored this finding. Given that the average distance between molecules in water is roughly ten times larger than this scale, we believe that thermal fluctuations are highly relevant in oceanic turbulence. In contrast, while we suspect the same may be true for atmospheric turbulence, the argument is less clear-cut due to the presence of condensation, which may reduce the importance of thermal fluctuations. To strengthen Betchov's prediction, we have performed direct numerical simulations of forced turbulence using a computational domain that can accommodate lengths up to $16\eta$, where $\eta$ is the Kolmogorov length. Our research reveals that when the Reynolds number is high enough, the mean dissipation ratio that drives the flow also reaches an equilibrium, allowing us to extend Betchov's prediction to any Reynolds number. Furthermore, by analyzing the flow's statistical properties, we have found that the average distance between molecules that drive the flow is closely related to the Kolmogorov length, even when the Reynolds number is extremely high. We have applied this relationship to estimate the impact of thermal fluctuations in the mesoscale, where the Reynolds number is around ten thousand. Our estimates suggest that thermal fluctuations play a significant role in this regime, with potential implications for

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient, a dimensionless quantity that cannot be derived from the Hall conductivity, as explained by recent findings. The origin of the magnetoelectric coefficient is analyzed for a time-reversal-symmetric system, and it is shown that it is based on an interaction between electrons that violates time-reversal symmetry. The time-reversal-symmetric component of the magnetoelectric coefficient can be understood by referring to two phenomena: the Witten effect, which occurs in a zero-dimensional topological insulator when a particle's wave function is rotated around a point with a magnetic monopole, and the half-integer quantum Hall effect, which appears when electrons are present in a two-dimensional layer and a magnetic field is applied perpendicular to it.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it's found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's map exhibits mode locking, characteristic of laminar chaos. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Conclusively determining the effectiveness of a design based on its requirements is a defined goal in natural language requirements mining. The requirement is considered met if a system design results in the desired conclusion. In this research, three different approaches to requirements mining were tested on the same dataset, with the final outcome being the same - all three methods consistently reached the same stable conclusion. Since the initial dataset was small and all three models reached the same stable conclusion, further studies can be conducted using the same framework with a larger dataset, potentially incorporating more sophisticated features.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent aspects of a superfluid/supersolid state.
Gravity emerges from topological defects within the post-inflation virtual "condensate" component.
Consequently, it is anticipated that exotic particles that could explain dark matter will not be detected at the LHC.
Instead, evidence for the model will emerge from observations of the universe's large-scale structure and its application to the black hole information paradox.

Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free byproduct, also enhancing the convergence rate once aligned with that of the problem's optimal solution. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not possible without adaptation. By assuming a proximal gradient method is able to recognize the differentiability manifolds in a nonparametric group of functions, we show that incorporating a quotient topology allows us to formally describe these manifolds and that a specific algorithm, based on Newton's method, achieves a similar convergence rate to that of optimal solutions. We support our theoretical findings with numerous numerical experiments, conducted on nonsmooth convex optimization problems with varying types of differentiability constraints.

We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is considered weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ whose product is contained in $I$, the sum of $a$ and $b$ is also in $I$. We are presenting a one-to-one correspondence between the set of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals in a ring and its nilpotent ideals of rank $2$, which is a specific type of $I$-nilpotent ideals. Furthermore, the properties of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals have been examined and their relationships with other prime ideals such as prime, strongly prime, and quasi-strongly prime ideals have been studied and compared.
