Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has the potential to contribute significantly to ongoing research in astronomy, particularly in studies of red dwarfs, brown dwarfs, and circumstellar envelopes.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

Several local authorities face challenges in deploying advanced automated
evaluation of road damage due to a lack of necessary technology, expertise, and
financial resources for sophisticated equipment. While countries like Japan have
introduced more cost-effective and accessible smartphone-based solutions for
automated road condition monitoring, many other countries continue to search for
efficient alternatives. To address these issues, this study contributes in
several key ways. Firstly, it examines the suitability of Japan's approach for
global implementation. Secondly, a substantial, multi-national smartphone-based
dataset consisting of 26,620 images is developed. Thirdly, a set of adaptable
models capable of detecting and classifying road damage in multiple countries is
proposed. Lastly, recommendations are provided for other countries seeking to
adopt successful strategies from their peers. The created dataset is available at
https://github.com/sekilab/RoadDamageDetector/.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation methods often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, when discrepancies arise between expert and agent domains due to varying dynamics, perspectives, or morphologies, imitation tasks become increasingly difficult.  This paper proposes a new framework that establishes correspondences across disparate domains using only unaligned trajectories containing states from the expert domain.  The framework leverages cycle-consistency constraints in both the state space and a domain-agnostic latent space to facilitate this correspondence.  Additionally, it ensures temporal alignment using a normalized position estimator.  Once the correspondence is established, the expert's actions can be directly imitated within the target domain.  The framework's performance is validated through experiments across a diverse range of complex domains.

A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We concentrate on how the initial star formation was influenced by magnetic effects in a cosmological setting with existing magnetic fields. We conducted a series of simulations of magnetohydrodynamics, running up to 1000 years following the initial protostar formation. To represent the protostars and their magnetic field structures, we utilized a stiff equation of state approach instead of the conventional sink particle technique. Ten years after the initial protostar formation, we observed an amplification in magnetic field strength from picogauss to kilogauss in the region around protostars, matching that of contemporary stars. Due to the rapid orbital rotations in the vicinity of protostars, their magnetic field became increasingly wound up over the initial decade of protostar formation. As mass accretion proceeded, the area where the magnetic field plays a crucial role in determining protostar formation expands outward and prevents the disk fragmentation observed in simulations with zero magnetic field. Conversely, in cases where gas clouds possess small angular momentum, we predict that amplification may be impaired because of decreased orbital speed; however, we note that disk fragmentation remains an impossibility under this condition. Ultimately, we determine that exponential amplification of the cosmological magnetic field from around 10^-18 G eliminates fragmentation of the disk

Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves partial implications between binary variables, which can be constrained by bounds such as support and confidence. When examining full implication bases consisting of very general associations, the concept of redundancy in association rules needs to be redefined. We investigate this problem by exploring existing definitions, proposing a novel characterization of redundancy, and highlighting its equivalence to concept preservation. We develop new results for association rule deducibility, construct optimal deduction schemes, and provide a method to identify the smallest possible bases consisting of association rules.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined the impact of a law requiring criminal defendants with mental health issues to participate in treatment.  The research found that those ordered to undergo treatment had a higher incidence of hospitalizations related to mental health than those without such orders.  An economic model suggested that forcing defendants with mental health issues to receive treatment lowered crime rates, particularly for those with severe mental illnesses.  However, this effect was not seen in cases of defendants without mental health issues.  An examination of hospital readmission data for individuals with mental health issues revealed that those under criminal justice system supervision and undergoing treatment had a higher incidence of mental health-related hospitalizations, and that the effect was most pronounced for individuals with more severe mental illnesses. The authors of the paper delve into various parameters that influence generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials, conducting initial examinations into their properties, such as generating functions, specific value calculations, and recurrence relations. The study further investigates parallel characteristics of the associated Bernoulli polynomials, highlighting significant differences.

Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip advanced wireless networks with situational awareness. They will likely serve a pivotal function in enabling UAV communications by allowing the assessment of signal strength and interference levels at unknown locations. Different from conventional radio map estimation techniques, which depend on uncontrolled sensor measurements, a new method proposes that a UAV collect data at designated locations along a carefully planned route to quickly obtain a reliable map. This research proposes an optimization algorithm for planning a sampling route that maximizes information gain for a simple scattering environment, and it is extended to a more complex environment with multiple scattering areas, where a novel heuristic is developed to efficiently plan a sampling route. Simulation results indicate that the proposed heuristic excels at both maximizing information gain and reducing sampling costs, even when operating at a low information-gaining rate of 50%.

This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and clustering techniques. At its core lies the comparison of sequential data segments. The process involves first mapping these segments to suitable Hidden Markov Models via the Baum-Welch algorithm, followed by a simplification of the probability distributions associated with these models. The resulting representation is then analyzed through a clustering method to pinpoint anomalies. Notably, the method functions effectively even in cases where the length of the data segments varies significantly. Our experiments, performed on synthetic data sets, as well as on real data from the power distribution sector, demonstrate that GLA surpasses or complements existing methods for detecting irregularities.

This research delves into a multi-aspect approach to person verification incorporating auditory, visual, and thermal modalities. Given the efficacy of auditory and visual modality combination, this investigation extends to exploring the effect of incorporating thermal images on verification robustness. Specifically, the contributors examine the performance enhancement achieved by integrating thermal modality, thereby enhancing scenario flexibility where visual information may be restricted. The multi-aspect verification system's efficiency is tested using the NIST 2018 Person dataset, with results showing improvements in performance with the inclusion of thermal images, provided that appropriate data alignment and feature extraction methods are employed.

Generating new training data through augmentation is achieved by appending existing examples to create new instances. We've found this approach to be both simple and cost-effective in boosting the performance of pre-optimized Transformer and Conformer models. Specifically, enhancements of up to 2.83 WER and 6.87 WER are seen in the LibriSpeech-960h test sets, and even higher when models were combined with fusion. Moreover, improvements of as much as 0.9 WER are recorded on the CoVoST-2 for several non-English languages following this training methodology. Notably, results indicate the magnitude of gain largely correlates with the size of initial training data. It is observed that our augmentation method can function effectively even when not utilizing speaker information. We've also demonstrated its effectiveness in translating spoken content into other languages by using this approach on multiple speech translation datasets.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in modeling experiments with random designs is illustrated through simulated data based on two-parameter scenarios, including the Burr XII distribution and its application to modeling interval times between events, as well as the use of empirical evidence in a real-world application for modeling data driven by the Pareto III distribution.

Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework by accounting for inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, the paper quantifies total privacy breaches when the adversary possesses record interdependence information, as well as demonstrates the creation of an optimization problem for an efficient trade-off between utility and privacy.

In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas and dust structures that resemble 'chemical gaps' created by the effects of radial-diffusion driven by the channeling inequity, despite these structures often being identical to'massive dust filters' formed by reduced dust sedimentation. We have observed a $^{12}C^{16}O$ gap in the AS 209 protoplanetary disk, located at 88 au, where we have found that the gas properties do not vary significantly from those at surrounding areas with smaller dust grains. We have made an observation that the gas surface density in the mid-plane could be higher than in surrounding areas with smaller dust grains by a factor of 0.72, indicating that the gas properties in the AS 209 disk do not show the characteristics of a 'chemical gap'. Instead, we propose that the structures formed in the AS 209 disk are actually a result of dust settlement, which has created conditions that allow us to study the formation of 10-my old planets under the magnifying glass.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. Since velocities are not directly observable in this model, we establish a key connection between control and velocity. Our analysis assumes a regularity condition on the Lagrangian and second-order Hamilton-Jacobi equation with a Lipschitz and convex regularity condition. This enables us to establish the existence of a common measure for control and velocity using Cannarsa and Capuani's method. Next, we show that both the control and velocity flows converge uniformly towards a path that satisfies the regular Hamilton-Jacobi equation, drawing from Ambrosio and Young's formula for calculating the flow's Lipschitz constant. Finally, we establish that the limit of the control flow corresponds to a control that optimizes the cost function.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial alignment as expected in real, interconnected structures, contrary to earlier assumptions. Calculating the masses of these structures based on their radial velocity dispersion revealed that they are actually not gravitationally bound. Furthermore, we found that these structures' ages, when compared to their actual age spread, appear excessively large. It is also worth noting that these structures, while seemingly homogeneous, can exhibit identical characteristics if composed of randomly selected stars from separate clusters, indicating that these structures might be mere coincidences. These findings call for a cautious interpretation of these structures' significance in understanding the star formation history of the Milky Way galaxy.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items don't match their outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we develop VICTOR from an explicit focus on visual incompatibility rather than relying on pre-trained image and language modalities. Empirical evaluations on two publicly available datasets demonstrate VICTOR's remarkable performance in detecting both visual incompatibilities and mismatched items, showcasing its potential for practical use in Outfit Maker apps.

The framework of quantum resource theory has significantly advanced quantum physics, enabling the unification of diverse methods to quantify specific quantum effects. It plays a pivotal role in optimizing their utility across various applications. The incorporation of radical quantum phenomena such as coherence, entanglement, and nonclassicality has enabled their application in real-world problems. The theoretical framework of quantum resource theory categorizes quantum states into 'free' and'resource' sets. Operations associated with free states emerge naturally from the system's constraints, whereas resource theories aim to discover and harness the potential within the restricted set. Recent advancements in the field see the adaptation of quantum resource theory to the description of optical fields, where the traditional assumptions of quantum mechanics are relaxed. The introduction of specific categorization tools, such as number states, allows experts to quantify the phase structure of optical fields and explore their applications across various experiments. This article serves as an introduction to the advancements in the field of optical quantum resource theory, presenting a comprehensive review of recent developments and their underlying mathematical concepts. We discuss the challenges and prospects of generalizing quantum resource theory beyond traditional quantum systems.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators.

Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude in the lower mass range. Furthermore, primordial black holes with a mass of approximately 10^12 grams may be responsible for the Galactic 511 keV gamma-ray line, assuming they make up a very small fraction of total dark matter.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both the collapse of the raft and the formation of voids can be easily measured. When we extend a raft of particles made of epoxy and glass microspheres beyond its equilibrium state, it enters a stage characterized by a non-linear decrease in area. This decrease occurs at a slower rate than its distance from the point of collapse, resulting in a widening gap. In the intermediate time regime before the onset of steady-state deformation, the distance to stability increases in a way that can be represented numerically. A steady-state that is characterized by a network of long and thin voids, surrounding stable and shape-dependent clusters of particles, is reached after a long time. The shape of these particle clusters varies based on the ratio of the particle diameter to the overall thickness of the raft. In the early stages of deformation, the rate at which the area decreases can be represented mathematically and numerically. This equation for the rate of area decrease applies across changes in the ratio of particle diameter to raft thickness. Our findings on the mechanics of a raft undergoing deformation may be related to problems in fluid dynamics and can serve as a reference point for designing materials with controlled voids.

The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In our investigation, we consider whether the mobility can be enhanced through epitaxial matching of GaN to certain II-IV nitride materials. We performed detailed computations utilizing the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation to evaluate the hole mobility of GaN, revealing that aligning GaN under uniaxial compressive strain by matching it to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ inorganic materials flips the order of the heavy and light hole bands, resulting in a reduced hole mass along the compression axis. Consequently, our calculations indicate that matching GaN to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ boosts its room temperature hole mobility by 50% and 260%, respectively, when compared to strain-free GaN. Furthermore, our study on the strain-mobility trends discloses a nonlinear correlation. Moreover, our model suggests that matching GaN to an imaginary solid solution composed of Zn$_{0.75}$Ge$_{0.75}$Mg$_{0.25}$Si$_{0.25}$N$_2$ could increase its hole mobility by 160%.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly increases data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and check for continuity in that region.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We modify its domain and demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This property allows us to estimate $P$ uniformly using finite-rank operators even when $P$ is not compact. We also establish that kernel-based techniques outperform traditional parametric methods like Galerkin methods in terms of convergence. Moreover, this research offers a new perspective on the limiting object of nonparametric regression operators.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on various $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. We explore alternative expressions for $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind by extending prior work on $\lambda$-analogues of unsigned or signed Stirling numbers of the second kind. We also establish several identities involving these specific $\lambda$-analogues. We draw analogies with existing identities for Stirling numbers of the second kind and $\lambda$-analogues of Stirling numbers of the first kind. We examine specific examples for $\lambda$-analogues of ${2}{k}$-stirling numbers of the second kind and provide a new recurrence relation that differs from the existing ${2}{k}$-stirling numbers of the first kind recurrence. We further discuss a different type of $\lambda$-analogues of ${2}{k}$-stirling numbers of the second kind where the lower parameter $\lambda$ is fixed and the upper parameter $r$ varies. We establish a different type of $\lambda$-analogues of ${2}{k}$-stirling numbers of the second kind where the lower parameter $\lambda$ is fixed and the upper parameter $r$ varies. We find that ${2}{k}$-stirling numbers of the second kind where $\lambda = \frac{1}{2}$ and $

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and existing models are limited in their ability to account for time. This paper presents a new concept called static models, which involves using time-sensitive vector representations of entities to improve link prediction accuracy. Our proposed method, static vector extension, involves augmenting existing static models with a time component, and can be applied without modifying the underlying model. Experimental results for 12 datasets demonstrate a general improvement in performance for this vector extension, and also highlight the potential for negative sampling to become a valuable research direction in knowledge graph enhancement.

This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence. This line of inquiry will likely hold significant value for ongoing research regarding infinite graphs and their associated C*-algebras. Moreover, this note specifically explores insplits and outsplits as key examples of strong shift equivalences, demonstrating that these equivalences lead to Morita equivalences that maintain consistency across various weighted gauge actions. Consequently, a question is raised about whether strong shift equivalence can be expressed as a product of insplits and outsplits.

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions.

To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices, thanks to the ability to infer new relationships between entities.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral properties. Our research involves taking an existing high dimensional expander X and generating a novel one, Y, within a specific ratio of dimensions, by incorporating vertices from the periphery of the covering spaces of X. By incorporating vertices from the periphery of the covering spaces of X, Our research demonstrates that taking an existing high dimensional expander X, we can produce a novel one, Y, within a specific ratio of dimensions, with a guarantee that Y's spectral properties will be at least as good as those of X. This innovative technique offers new avenues for constructing high dimensional expanders and understanding the general bounds on its spectral properties, with additional implications for constructing high dimensional embeddable complexes.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those based on reasoning styles exhibit notable variations in performance. These findings offer practical implications for both the automatic generation of prompts and the way humans create them to accomplish a particular task.

We have computed the $\mathscr{L}$-invariants of weight one cycles in a finite regulo-Lusong prime $p$ for the big Artin tree. We have further proved that the cyclotomic $\mathscr{L}$-invariants of weight one cycles are interconnected with the eigenvarieties of overconvergent Hilbert spaces.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise, but accurately distinguishing between thousands of MW 
frequencies is a challenge that surpasses current technological capabilities. 
We've taken a major step forward in this area of study by successfully 
recognizing over 200 frequency pairs simultaneously using Rydberg atoms and 
deep learning methods, which may lead to new possibilities in MW radar and 
communication systems.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint.

Using the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer on board the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile Evolution/NASA Mars Science Laboratory mission, the oscillating CO$_{2}$ density in the upper Martian atmosphere, spanning between 120 and 190~km in altitude, is monitored. This observation is carried out for about 606~days when the atmospheric conditions are stable and quiet. In conjunction with the Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory mission's gravity data, the properties of the upper atmospheric waves, namely their amplitudes, propagation directions, and vertical and horizontal scales, are determined. Those properties are further compared with the local gravity wave growth theory and verified using the Mars Science Laboratory's shadow imaging. Additionally, the characteristics of the upper atmospheric waves as obtained from the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer are compared with the findings of the Mars Odysseus Orbiter's Neutral Gas analyzer, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's Neutral Gas analyzer, and the Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution mission's Neutral Gas analyzer. Some discrepancies and differences in the data are explained and highlighted.

The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, acting as a source of photons, which can then interact either with other photons or with hadrons. Specifically, ultra-peripheral collisions occur when high-energy ions surpass the range of the strong force, enabled by virtual photons exchanged between the nuclei, whose numbers directly correlate with nuclear electric charge. Given its exceptional energy levels, the LHC serves as the most powerful photon source ever constructed, particularly in favouring photoproduction of heavy vector mesons due to their inherent affinity to photons. Recent experiments examining the forward J/psi production in lead-lead ultra-peripheral collisions at 5.02 TeV using the ALICE detector are featured.

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, discrete sound segments and letting the model generate a full audio track. However, the quality of the resulting audio is highly sensitive to the selection of these sound segments, which can be time-consuming to identify. We propose a more efficient approach, presenting a model that takes visual footage and generates a full audio track in one continuous process. We also introduce a new loss function, the 'Semitone' loss, to improve the accuracy of the generated sound labels. Comprehensive evaluations on existing sound generation datasets demonstrate our model's ability to outperform current benchmarks and produce high-quality audio with accurate sound labels. An audio demo is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K9QkKEh7g14.

Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including time-series information and natural language. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context information. This enables recurrent neural networks to learn complex temporal patterns, making them particularly well-suited for tasks such as stock market forecasting, speech recognition, and language modeling. Key components of these models include memory cells, recurrence relationships, and the incorporation of input information. By maintaining a temporal context, these networks can learn sequential patterns, even taking advantage of long-term memory properties. This temporal context is typically managed through one of three primary memory cell types: simple, cell-and-gate, or long short-term memory cells. In this chapter, we delve into the fundamentals of recurrent neural networks, discussing variants such as LSTM and GRU, as well as key algorithms for learning model parameters. Additionally, we examine applications of recurrent neural networks in sequence prediction and relevant benchmark datasets.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes this finding to the broader concept of 'economic irreversibility,' illustrating its analogy to the principles of thermodynamics. A fundamental inequality provides a framework for the implementation of such measures. A novel theoretical approach underlying this methodology contributes to the body of econophysics research.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is heavily reliant on a complex pipeline of data-based processing stages. Yet, the efficacy of these models is consistently hindered by issues stemming from the data they utilize. It's clear that some data subsets contribute positively, while others may pose significant risks by introducing bias, inequity, or incomplete coverage. However, identifying and quantifying these problems across various stages of the pipeline remains a significant challenge. To address this problem, we introduce a novel approach called SLP- $\Delta$, an adaptive debugging system capable of sending flow-controlled data probes through the pipeline to yield meaningful insights into model performance. To enhance scalability, we develop a proprietary optimization algorithm linked to the Shapley value framework, allowing for efficient evaluation of data importance. Our proposed method is tested on real-world scenarios involving synthetic and actual datasets, and we highlight its practical applications for both debugging and model fine-tuning tasks.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa, the material's anomalous Hall effect is entirely eliminated. The pressure-dependent magnetization study revealed that as pressure increased, Mn$_3$Sn shifted from a conventional antiferromagnetic ground state to a helical state, where a required characteristic for the anomalous Hall effect is absent. The structural changes associated with this transition were confirmed through high-resolution x-ray diffraction, where a pronounced shift in Bragg peaks was observed at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa. The investigation further revealed that as pressure increased, the material's core structure underwent significant changes, where a pronounced (220) reflection emerged at pressures exceeding 1.2 GPa, while its (111) reflection disappeared at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa. The material's temperature-dependent magnetic properties were found to be dependent on pressure, with specific magnetic transitions occurring at distinct pressures. The entire pressure range was found to exhibit a 3.5% volume expansion, where the material's core structure underwent significant changes. The experiment was repeated three times, where the pressure

Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By automatically
identifying semantic relationships between entities, RE contributes significantly to
domain-independent knowledge reasoning. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have emerged as
a preferred choice for RE. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of
deep learning-based RE methods by addressing essential aspects such as data representation,
hyper-parameter tuning, and model generalizability, in addition to highlighting current
challenges and potential future research directions.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informing our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. Through our analysis of two benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that hypergraph projections conceal essential characteristics, but incorporating expert knowledge can significantly enhance the reconstruction of a hypergraph's properties. Our supervised hypergraph reconstruction approach, which integrates expert information via edge-label projections, yields superior results compared to a naive method in preserving the connectivity structure of the original hypergraph. The exceptional performance of our method suggests that hypergraph projections, being readily available for many applications, offer a viable means to investigate the structural properties of complex systems.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe the inner body structures. Preparing these reports necessitates medical
experts to be familiar with both normal anatomy and the detection of anomalies.
Current medical image analysis systems lack the knowledge of anatomical structure
appearance due to difficulty in collecting annotated data, thus restricting their
capability to narrow expertise areas, like diagnosing specific conditions. Our
research addresses this gap by incorporating human anatomy and allowing the
connection between report content and corresponding image content. To utilize
anatomical information, we introduce an advanced system to gather and integrate
human body structures from CT scans and incorporate it into PAXRay. The latter is
a comprehensive dataset for X-Ray anatomical structure segmentation. Our results
show that employing anatomical information significantly enhances visually linking
radiologists' observations with images, as our segmentations result in a 50%
better grounding outcome on the OpenI dataset compared to commonly used region
proposal methods. The PAXRay dataset, with its extensive range of anatomical
structures, is accessible at https://constantinseibold.github.io/PAXRay/.

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range and then made an educated guess that this range is the absolute minimum. Subsequent work by a different researcher, collaborating with David Gabai, found counterexamples that contradict this theory. Due to the connection between tight contact structures and taut foliations, researchers now consider the possibility that this theory could hold for tight contact structures, which are also related to Euler classes of one. To test this idea, recent findings show that previously found counterexamples are also related to tight contact structures, suggesting the theory may be valid for these structures.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle angular distributions with multiple peaks. Conversely, entropy based on differential uncertainty already achieves optimal results for emission directionality without being confined to basic scenarios, making it a more versatile method.

Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and four major stock indexes. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a strong connection among the returns of leading cryptocurrencies and their counterparts. Secondly, the results of multiple statistical tests, performed using similar data from 2015 to 2017 as a reference, confirmed that the filtered returns in the subsequent three-year period did not differ significantly. Finally, the application of spectral density estimations revealed the presence of common trends among the returns of leading cryptocurrencies and their counterparts. Our findings were consistently robust in the presence of various models describing the price dynamics of cryptocurrencies.

By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation at early time periods. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which reformulates large deviations into a nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, we reveal its complete solvability through a link with the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Employing the inverse scattering technique and a newly developed Fredholm determinant framework, we arrive at exact solutions that depend on the specific initial conditions of the KPZ equation, allowing for further generalization to other initial conditions.

The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed with data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe, researchers are able to investigate turbulent patterns down to specific frequencies. These measurements are then applied to various solar wind plasma intervals. One such interval is scrutinized, yielding valuable insights into its power spectral density fluctuations spanning from the inertial to sub-ion range. Two possible explanations for these density patterns exist, suggesting that they are a result either of specific wave types and interactions at varying scales or a broader physical phenomenon, the Hall effect. These theories are substantiated through the examination of associated electric field data.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts, with a potential for delivering over a thousand pulses per second to enable groundbreaking attosecond science applications.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which leverages fabric orientation information. By integrating the fabric direction map, GHOG extends the conventional SOG, enabling more precise detection of defects with varied orientations. Building on this, a low-rank decomposition technique is employed to differentiate and isolate defects from background pixels in fabric images, effectively disabling the influence of background noise. Consequently, a sparse matrix representing only fabric defects is obtained and utilized for defect localization. Notably, this method exhibits superior accuracy and efficiency compared to traditional methods, demonstrating robust results even on images with intricate backgrounds.

To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to simulate the impact of its actions, leveraging this understanding to forecast the outcome of different navigational choices. As a result, the agent achieves improved cross-target and cross-scene generalization capabilities, outperforming current state-of-the-art models by at least 10% according to AI2-THOR evaluations. Our method demonstrates real-world efficacy through successful navigation in diverse environments, including continuous video navigation and holistic 3D world exploration.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the reionization of the universe. Our framework accounts for the spatial distribution of the first stars with a mass of $10^2$ to $10^6$ $M_{\odot}$ each, resulting in 30 - 300 compact objects with a mass of $10^2$ $M_{\odot}$ each that form a binary with a separation of ~100-1000 $P_c$ (the gravitational wave radius). These binaries reside within the densest regions of the cluster and their merger events produce gravitational waves with amplitudes exceeding that of GW150914. The overall frequency content and abundance of these events resemble that of supernovae-derived mergers. Additionally, our model suggests that the frequency range and characteristic strain of these Population III mergers could be detectable by future gravitational wave detectors like LISA, with a signal-to-noise ratio exceeding 10 for ~10% of the mergers and a likelihood of >50% for those with frequencies less than 10^{-4} Hz. Furthermore, the observations by LISA could be used to determine the mass density of the universe and a relationship exists between the ionization fraction and the mass of the binary.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on active and reactive power control strategies for ESS.

Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$. The first process is predominantly driven by the $\omega$ meson. On the other hand, the cascade decays involving the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons are substantially suppressed compared to other diagrams, specifically those that go through the $\psi(2S)$ or a three-body decay of $\rho$. The measured branching ratios for $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ are potentially within reach for the BESIII and LHCb Collaborations. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ decays may be used to determine the couplings $g_{X\psi\omega}$ and $g_{X\psi\rho}$, respectively, which would offer insights into the isoscalar and isovector components of the X(3872) wave function.

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

The study on varying electron spin orientation employs the coordinate transformation method. Characteristically, Topological Insulators exhibit an uneven spin orientation shift within the Brillouin zone. In cases of defects, this shift occurs along closed paths in real space, with the topological quantity measured through the electron spin's wind-turning around this path. A geometric analysis of the electron spin's motion across the lattice structure reveals that the presence of defects gives rise to a torsional force, causing the electron spin to twist. This force quantitatively determines the spin's wind-turning around any given path in real space.

u$ ranges between 0.5 and infinity, and $\mathcal{S}_
u$ denotes the set of non-zero vectors in 2D space with a polar angle smaller than $ rac{\pi}{2
u}$. We introduce $R > 0$, and $\omega_p^R$ as the cone-based solution to the $p$-Laplace equation, both in its standard form and when modified with a Dirichlet boundary condition, within the region between the line with angle $ rac{\pi}{2
u}$ and radius $R$, and the half-plane to its left. We show that for any given point $x$ within this region, the ratio of the magnitude of the function to the distance between the point and the line with angle $ rac{\pi}{2
u}$, raised to the power of $ rac{
u}{
u-1}$, serves as an upper bound for the magnitude of the function at that point. We also demonstrate that for small distances between the point and the line with angle $ rac{\pi}{2
u}$, the function behaves similarly to its behavior at the origin, and for larger distances, the function decreases proportionally to the magnitude of the angle. We present various examples to illustrate the bounds we introduced, as our estimates remain valid for all values of $p$, and further, the lower bound we provided,

Using a multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers.

Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-dependent information, significantly contributing to teaching robots human-like motion through emulation. In robotics literature, there is a prevalent assumption that manipulability tensors and their associated Riemannian structures remain stationary and unaffected by changes in position, orientation, and planning variables, a notion we disproved in this research. The lack of robust modeling methods to capture these tasks' geometric complexities results in robots failing to replicate human motions accurately. To address this issue, we developed a novel paradigm to adapt manipulability learning from a trainer's repertoire to another user with different manipulability requirements, carrying out the transfer under the guidance of visual feedback. The proposed approach involves transporting the trainer's manipulability tensor to the patient's frame using Parallel Transport, then aligning the resulting tensor via a pose estimation technique called Manifold-ICP, to ensure optimal alignment of the tensor's underlying geometric structure. Empirical evaluations on real and simulated datasets validated the efficacy of our method, demonstrating pose accuracy within millimeters and pose alignment accuracy of 98.7%, posing a significant improvement over existing methods.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a result, we were able to achieve a $0.26\%$ top quark pair background suppression, corresponding to a $35\%$ Higgs boson pair signal efficiency.

A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video footage where objects are rotated. These scenes are commonly encountered and can be easily gathered (e.g. cars navigating roundabouts, planes near airfields). The combination of traditional structure-from-motion techniques and cutting-edge object detection and feature matching methods yields surprisingly accurate 3D pose estimations in such video footage. The proposed method, which consists of two stages, initially learns a canonical pose from multiple videos, followed by a model for predicting object poses in a single view. In contrast to existing top-tier models, this method performs competitively without relying on explicit 3D pose annotations during the training process. Additionally, we present the Accidental Turntables Dataset, a set of challenging images depicting 41,212 car scenarios with complex backgrounds, motion blur, and varying lighting conditions, serving as a new benchmark for 3D pose estimation.

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can discern one's attitude toward this misinformation. This new framework leverages neural networks and attitude consistency to classify stances toward COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. A novel neural framework, utilizing knowledge graphs to organize stances, successfully identifies attitudes toward this misinformation with outstanding results, particularly outperforming competing approaches on a newly created extensive dataset consisting of conversations between doctors and patients.

Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to unveil the core electronic behavior of matter, contingent on achieving two interconnected technological milestones linked to high-order harmonic generation sources. Firstly, achieving a higher photon flux would allow researchers to measure even the faintest electronic processes, while also attaining better spectral tunability would grant selectivity in targeting specific electronic transitions. Breakthroughs are made feasible by parametric waveform synthesis, giving scientists the capability to craft controllable, highly-tunable high-energy electric transients. Our findings demonstrate that by manipulating the waveform of the driving laser pulse via its relative phase and carrier-envelope phase, it's possible to exert fine-grained control over attosecond pulse characteristics. This innovation not only amplifies experimental possibilities in the realm of attosecond science, but also paves the way for a highly sophisticated, coherent manipulation of free-electron paths.

Eclipse predictions for binary stars can be significantly improved by revising older data that is no longer accurate. This involves accounting for potential companions that can create recurring periods in time shifts. A study discovered a low probability (0.00005%) of detecting new companions using eclipse time shifts. Researchers analyzed data on Algol ($\beta$ Persei) and found tentative signs of up to five additional companion candidates, which are believed to have orbital periods ranging from 1.863 to 219 years. These signals are consistent across 236 years of data and also matched the first 226.2 years of the data, accurately predicting eclipses for the following 9.2 years. The companion candidates' orbital planes are thought to be aligned due to the stable and unchanging eclipses of Algol since the early observations of Goodricke (1783).

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency are required for this approach. To address this need, enhancing training point generation is an important direction of investigation. Both adaptive and quasi-uniform methods have inherent drawbacks - the former can lead to inaccurate solution approximation, while the latter may result in unnecessary computational expense. In response, we introduce a new method called Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, which combines the positive aspects of these techniques. Specifically, we utilize an approximation error estimator to identify areas requiring additional nodes, and these new nodes are positioned using a meshless method that optimizes distance between nodes. As a result, the RANG approach yields computational efficiency improvements of at least 2-fold compared to both traditional and advanced adaptive methods. Furthermore, it also offers at least a 2-fold improvement in computational efficiency over the quasi-uniform approach.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the oscillations in their electrostatic conduction band profile, which are characteristic of these devices. We model these dynamics by solving coupled two-dimensional Poisson's equations and energy equations, and find that the system converges to a stable thermodynamic state through energy minimization. Our analysis also shows that the movement of domain walls within the ferroelectric material leads to the negative capacitance effect, which in turn affects the device's drain current and variability due to the domain period. We also investigated how the domain wall's soft or hard state transition influences the device's electrical properties and transport. Our simulations are verified through both experimental data and phase-field modeling.

A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and how vulnerability dissemination occurs within it. Unlike other ecosystems like Maven and NuGet, Cargo's distinct architecture and communication mechanisms differ from those of other ecosystems. This research aims to address these questions by constructing a novel knowledge graph in Cargo and investigating the spread of vulnerabilities. Our approach involves creating a graph with dependencies and vulnerability domains, enabling the study of vulnerability dissemination through graph analysis. By examining the Cargo ecosystem's structure and vulnerability spread methods, we uncover insights such as the central roles of certain libraries, the prevalence of vulnerability dissemination occurring within the same language, and the limited impact of direct project dependencies on vulnerability dissemination. This research provides Cargo ecosystem stakeholders with valuable insights to inform best practices and guidelines for securing the ecosystem.

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to demonstrate irreducibility. This paper confirms the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subjected to discrete jump noises and shows these results apply universally, imposing minimal restrictions on noise conditions. A critical factor in this study is the authors' and T. Zhang's previously established criteria for irreducibility in stochastic equations with jump noises. This proof is then utilized to demonstrate ergodic behavior in stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations and includes scenarios of weak dissipation with jump degenerate noise.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This power graph connects vertices based on one being a positive power of the other. By examining the group's prime divisors and Sylow subgroups, we've pinpointed vertices related to its cyclic subgroups. This allows us to establish a connection between the group's properties and its minimal vertex degree in the power graph. This study provides degree calculations for specific types of noncyclic abelian groups.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively studied at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 GeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the characteristics of cosmic ray showers.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing a matrix factorization framework with sparsity and low-rank constraints to integrate local and global structures. Through the propagation of this low-rank structure, our method achieves significantly improved sparsity for representing the original Gabor filter bank. Our experimental results show that OCNs outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and computational cost, with a significant reduction in model complexity.

This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron component, and introduce two effective modifications. Firstly, we substitute the conventional KNN search with a DiracI CN distance-based method, which significantly reduces complexity and pruning frequency. Additionally, we introduce a novel downsampled feature aggregation (DFAS) technique for GCNs, aiming to decrease the number of times features are aggregated in the network. Both of these modifications significantly boost the computational efficiency of GCNs. Our method outperforms existing approaches, such as SPGN, EGCN, and CSRGN, in terms of accuracy, while also demonstrating general applicability to various point cloud learning tasks. The source code of this work can be found at https://github.com/chenyizheng/DFAS_GCNs.

We introduce a groundbreaking form of Trojan attack, which exploits neural network embeddings to bypass trigger detection without relying on specific inputs. Our approach, which can be applied to various embedding techniques including CNN and transformer-based models, allows for the deployment of universal backdoors on pre-trained models without requiring modification of the model itself. The key components of our method are semantic backdoor triggers and trigger cleaners, which work together to conceal the Trojan trigger even when the model encounters similar triggers in future episodes. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this method against existing defense mechanisms, particularly for text-based models, and highlight its potential for long-term applications in natural language processing systems.

We are developing an image slicer for an integral field unit, ROSIE IFU, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. By splitting the 50.4 x 53.5 field of view into four subfields, and further segmenting these into 21 individual 0.6 x 53.5 slices, we'll achieve four pseudo-slits, spaced six arcminutes apart. This will allow for a spectral range of 1800 Angstroms with a resolution of 2000. Our current progress includes preparing the optics, coating the first slicer, crafting the mounts, and writing the software, all aiming to enhance IMACS's functionality by facilitating the efficient examination of expansive astronomical objects like galaxies and nebulae.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) are considered to outline the pathway for enhancing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations via new Threshold Hand Mirror (THM) measurements.

A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets with compositions similar to those of Earth. New findings from a study of eight stars that host terrestrial planets are presented, focusing on the structural and compositional properties of the planets. By analyzing the elemental abundances of these stars, researchers obtained accurate mass and radius estimates for the planets, using theoretical models of their interiors. This enabled calculations of a planetary parameter indicating the likelihood of a rocky or icy composition. Planets with high metallicities were found to have a high probability of being made of rocky material, as they can form from normal to super-stoichiometric amounts of rock more easily than those with lower metallicities. The parameter showed a correlation with planetary mass, with lower-mass planets being more likely to be made of rocky material and higher-mass planets having a higher chance of being made of icy material. This study's results demonstrate the potential for characterizing the compositions of terrestrial planets using elemental abundances in their host stars.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict the potential of channel representation learning by the DNN. This research suggests attention-based CSI for learning robust features.
