The proposed approach's efficacy in centralized and distributed massive MIMO systems is assessed using ray-tracing channels in two railway environments under varying conditions, resulting in a superior performance compared to a conventional DNN.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework.

In 1980, Faudree, Schelp, and Tuza proposed a conjecture stating that every cubic bipartite graph has a strong $2$-edge-coloring. This means if we assign different colors to edges according to a specific rule, ensuring no adjacent edges have the same color, and apply this coloring to all edges, the resulting arrangement would be a planar graph. Over the years, researchers attempted to verify this statement but were unsuccessful. In this research, we present a counterexample disproving the Faudree-Schelp-Tuza conjecture.

We investigate functions defined on the vertices of the Hamming graphs H(n,q), focusing specifically on those with support contained in the union of all spheres of radius r centered at the identity. It's shown that for a function f with domain H(n,q), an upper bound exists for the size of its support when its Fourier coefficients up to a certain level are zero. This upper bound is closely related to the value of n, r, and q. In cases where the Fourier spectrum is limited to a single layer or two, tight bounds are established for the size of a function's support. It's also shown that for functions on H(n,q), certain combinations of spectral constraints and parameters n, r, and q can be covered by an identical upper bound for the size of a function's support.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables running tasks available in the original software within a browser. It offers a basic model upload feature and a server-loaded model option, providing web access to existing models. Users can access ShinyCOPASI at http://shiny.copasi.org/ and the source code at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent advancements, the systematic quantification of uncertainty remains a pressing issue in the field. This work addresses that need by investigating various methods for quantifying uncertainty in NN predictions, introducing enhancements to existing techniques, and identifying priorities for future research. The study utilizes a novel set of benchmark problems designed to test different aspects of uncertainty quantification. A comprehensive comparison of the reported results reveals that, when faced with limited data, NN estimates are often comparable to those of classical methods but are consistently superior with larger data sets. The work presents theoretical analysis, derivations, and empirical evidence highlighting the potential for improved decision-making in physics-based deep learning applications.

We are investigating quantum group analogues of the free group factors' radial subalgebras, specifically those of class functions, within the context of compact quantum groups. We found that the algebras of class functions for the free orthogonal quantum groups cannot be maximally abundant *-subalgebras (MASAs) under certain conditions. Central to our research is the concept of a quasi-split inclusion. We demonstrated that the inclusion of the class functions' algebra is quasi-split in certain unitary quantum group scenarios. Additionally, we showed that the resulting subalgebra is non-abelian. We obtained another key finding related to its relative commutant in such instances. In contrast, we constructed specific bicrossed products based on $SU_q(2)$ for which the class functions' algebra constitutes a MASA.

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees, was introduced. This method is further exemplified through inexact GMRES policy iteration, which applies GMRES for the policy evaluation process. Notably, inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms policy iteration and optimistic policy iteration by 5.8 and 2.2 times, respectively, in a 10000-state MDP.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior.

This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive-to-evaluate time-series simulators. Specifically, we investigate the case where a simulator generates output data as a multi-dimensional time series for various input parameters. Our goal is to determine the optimal parameter setting that yields the best match with real measurement data. Given the high cost and multi-dimensional nature of these simulators, traditional modeling approaches are impractical. We propose a solution by treating the simulation output as a function to be visualized and navigating its relationship with the real data through visualization. However, since we are dealing with large datasets, direct visualization is not feasible, and we employ a method of reducing the complexity of the data while preserving key relationships, and then apply a technique of iterative estimation and visualization. This approach offers a efficient solution with guaranteed accuracy. Our case studies demonstrate that the proposed method delivers a effective outcome and outperforms other methods in terms of computational efficiency.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and considering the influence of random example exposure, according to Gourdeau et al. (2021). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first distribution-free algorithms for achieving robust empirical risk minimization, a challenging problem in learning robust models. We prove that, in contrast to previous results, having access to local queries suffices to solve this problem, where the number of queries needed scales polynomially and exponentially depending on the number of relevant attributes in the input data. To achieve this goal, we adapt the robust learning algorithm from Gourdeau et al. (2021) and introduce new components of robust learning from random examples. We also investigate the exact amount of information that can be learned through random example exposure and show that existing algorithms' performance depends on the number of relevant attributes in the input data. Furthermore, we experimentally verify the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms on synthetic and real-world data.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV were tracked within a narrow cone around the jet axis. By pairing with a high-transverse-momentum photon, the trajectory of the parent parton can be well constrained. In central lead-lead collisions, variations in fragmentation functions compared to those measured in proton-proton collisions were detected, however, little deviation was seen in collisions occurring outside the 50% most central range. Jets within the central lead-lead events exhibited a higher yield of low-energy particles, paired with a decrease in high-transverse-momentum particles, roughly transitioning at a point around 3 GeV. This study is the first to demonstrate alterations in parton (dominated by quarks) showers traversing the QGP with a known initial trajectory, also offering a controlled comparison to test theoretical models.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts.

Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, has yielded an assortment of peculiar attributes for the object. New images taken by Keck/MOSFIRE and HST/WFC3 cameras have established that the object is among a select few with extremely faint proper motion, indicating it has a temperature under 150 K. Moreover, the object possesses a distinct pattern of spectral features in the J, H, and K bands, featuring prominent absorption lines associated with CH4 and PH3 molecules. The object's luminosity in the W1 band is reported to be 7.47 mag, with an estimated mass between 2 and 9 times the mass of Jupiter and an age of approximately 700 million years. The researchers consider the object to either possess a very low-mass companion with a brown dwarf or ultracool dwarf properties. If the low surface brightness is a companion's influence, the companion would need to be situated very close to the object, under 0.2 AU. Alternatively, the surface brightness could be the outcome of a brown dwarf's low surface gravity, in which case the object would need to be a brown dwarf with low surface gravity.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on the final state particle multiplicity. Data are compared to Pb-Pb and
Pb-Xe relativistic nuclear collision results from the Large Hadron Collider, and a relative
production decrease of $\Sigma p$ mesons and a relative increase of $\pi^0$ mesons 
observed relative to Pb-Pb collisions. Also, the observed enhancement of the $\phi$ 
meson over expectations for peripheral Xe-Xe collisions is noted.

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and flavor matching.

Specimens made of Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, in the form of cylinders, were created using a combination of saltwater and heat, and then fired at various temperatures to analyze their internal structure, strength and contraction. The internal structures of these materials were studied under a microscope and their mechanical properties were tested using a universal testing machine. The experiment was performed twice using different types of simulants for Martian and Lunar soil, resulting in manufactured samples resembling traditional building blocks and the initial stages of 3D printing with a binder. The results indicated that the optimal firing temperature for both types of simulants lies between 1100 C and 1200 C. The compressive strength of these materials met the requirements for building structures on other planets, suggesting their potential for use as building materials in extraterrestrial construction and as a base material for additive manufacturing processes similar to 3D printing with a binder.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This research investigates the effect of a non-wetting liquid on a fiber, considering the variability of the liquid-solid angle under different conditions. By applying the axisymmetric drop model, we analyzed the dynamics of a narrow liquid film on a fiber, observing its slip-enhanced instability in contrast to situations where such slip does not occur. Moreover, we found that increased liquid-solid angle values lead to shorter times for the liquid film to completely disappear. Additionally, we examined the role of liquid-surface tension and liquid density on the liquid film dynamics. Lastly, we compared our theoretical findings to a study using the lattice Boltzmann method, validating the axisymmetric drop model's applicability for certain liquid film states.

By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST.

This is the first part of a two-part investigation into a category of quantum deformations, specifically focusing on the properties of a category of modules derived from a process called type II induction from the special type of algebras, called type I quantum subgroups, in the complex representation of a significant group of algebraic structures, denoted as $\mathfrak{sl}_{N}$. By drawing on information about the extremal type of algebras associated with integral orbits of a significant group of algebraic structures, acting on a significant group of algebraic structures, denoted as $\mathfrak{sl}_{N}$, we have found that this category of modules has certain properties similar to those of extremal type of algebras, and this is further explained through the discussion of the extremal type of algebras associated with integral orbits of a significant group of algebraic structures, in the second part of the investigation.

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome that contradicts conventional travelling wave approximations commonly utilised in the field.

This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to classify handwritten mathematical terms based on time series data from the DigiPen. The challenge involves recognizing mathematical expressions from 15 possible characters written by multiple individuals. To overcome the initial challenge, a data-driven and rule-based information extraction technique is applied to break down the labeled data. Following this process, two machine learning models are developed - the first is a binary classifier leveraging a hybrid Deep Neural Network and Random Forest to detect writing activities, and the second is a Deep Neural Network integrating convolutional and recurrent layers for single-character classification. Although the proposed approach demonstrates satisfactory accuracy and performance in the challenge evaluation simulation with an average Levensthein Distance of 8, its overall efficiency and real-time capabilities still require improvement.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers an adaptable solution for speech synthesis due to its ability to produce a variety of distribution types over time. An evaluation on a large speech corpus indicates that this approach surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in terms of the diversity of generated speech lengths.

Species distribution analysis can be effectively conducted through occupancy modeling, taking into consideration inaccuracies in species detection data. To address multiple species, states, interactions, false positives, autocorrelation, and data from various sources, various modifications to the fundamental single species occupancy model have been introduced. However, creating high-performance software that can analyze large spatial data sets is still a developing field. A newly developed package, spOccupancy for R, is designed to fit single, multiple species, and combined occupancy models that are sensitive to spatial relationships. Utilizing a Bayesian approach with Pólya-Gamma data augmentation and Gaussian Process neighbor techniques, this package enables efficient model computation even for extensive datasets. spOccupancy provides intuitive functionalities for simulating data, testing models, verifying predictions, evaluating model performance, and making predictions on unseen data. Through a case study and a tutorial, this package demonstrates its capabilities by estimating species abundance in two distinct bird habitats: eastern USA's bird population and a forest ecosystem in New Hampshire, thereby providing a practical approach to address data inaccuracies and spatial relationships even for extensive datasets.

Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Moreover, studies have shown that general practitioners make fewer accurate diagnoses compared to artificial intelligence. The Skincare project aimed to address this by creating an innovative diagnostic and decision support system in dermatology. It combined the capabilities of interactive machine learning with deep learning to enhance the skills of doctors and augment diagnostic capabilities, particularly in the identification of malignant skin lesions. A baseline model, trained using a large dermatology image dataset (ISIC), delivered outstanding results and demonstrated potential for widespread application, as it could be adapted for use on mobile devices and medical staff with various skill levels. The project also explored applications in education and implemented a platform for gathering, processing, and visualizing clinical data. Ultimately, the Skincare project sought to integrate interactive machine learning and deep learning into clinical practice, ultimately improving patient outcomes.

To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that incorporates a Normalizing Flow component after initial training using an Auto-Encoder. The model's two-stage generative architecture, comprising a deterministic and a stochastic component, effectively models real data after being regularized using a KL-unifier. In a novel approach, we use a type of regression analysis called Proportional to Distance, or PD, to align the SVD-based latent representations of our model with the standard phase points of type Ia supernovae. The results show that this method enables our model to generate coherent spectral time-series data, even when only a single snapshot is available for each supernova. Furthermore, we found that our model's representation system, comprising the standard phase points and the SVD-bases, effectively distinguishes between genuine and artificial supernovae. A mock sample analysis demonstrated that our model performs well in a variety of statistical tasks. The project's website contains further details and the ability to download the code, data and other required resources.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been observed in a gravitationally lensed star-forming galaxy. The outflow is visible in a specific OH+ absorption line, which was measured by the ALMA telescope at high spatial resolution. The data also include CO emission, dust, and stellar light. Analysis of the outflow shows that it has different properties than other gas outflows seen in similar galaxies. The outflow's mass loss rate, kinetic energy, and energy budget are studied and compared to other gas outflows. The outflow's properties are in line with those seen in similar galaxies but its impact on star formation is uncertain. The outflow's effects on its surrounding galaxy and the conditions necessary for feedback are also considered. The observations of this galaxy provide a clear picture of a massive outflow and can help inform theoretical studies. The outflow's properties can be adjusted based on the galaxy's characteristics and can inform the use of feedback models in simulations. The outflow's impact on the galaxy's evolution can be determined by studying its mass loss rate and kinetic energy over time. The outflow's direction may play a role in its feedback on the galaxy's evolution. The outflow's density and temperature can inform the use of feedback models in simulations. The outflow's pressure can inform models of the galaxy's evolution and its effect on the surrounding intergalactic medium.

To study the movement of fluid into a swirling, turbulent plume containing heavy particles that scatter equally in all directions, researchers used a computational model. This model assumed the plume has constant properties and that the particles affect the fluid's movement only when they are near the plume's center. By accounting for the particles' presence, the model determined that the fluid moves faster into the plume compared to a situation without particles, with the amount of increase depending on the particles' size. This effect was observed regardless of the particles' density. If the particles are smaller than the differences in density between the fluid and the surrounding air, they cause a convective instability within the plume, which is then steeper than a typical turbulent plume. Additionally, the problem is scaled and the particles' size is analyzed for how it affects different aspects of the fluid's movement.

Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting hyperedges to model these interactions, we create more comprehensive models, allowing the transmission rate to depend on the number of infectious contacts a person has. This approach leads us to develop new spectral conditions and study various types of contagion models, considering both the stochastic individual-level model and the mean-field approximation. Numerical examples and the analysis that follows enable the differentiation between inherent disease characteristics and the impact of individual actions. Ultimately, this framework holds potential for a more precise evaluation of the effectiveness of virus containment interventions.

Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of the CrI$_3$ layer, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics.  Investigating the properties of the CrI$_3$ bilayer using state-of-the-art computational techniques, researchers found that this model exhibits an array of intricate spin textures, including local curvature and global patterns, arising from interplay of ferromagnetic ordering and charge imbalance.  Contrary to expectations, they discovered that the most lower energy states exhibit ferromagnetic ordering rather than an anti-ferromagnetic arrangement.  Additionally, the most stable configuration features a non-zero net magnetic moment, a finding that contradicts initial experimental observations.  Crucially, they found that inter-layer coupling in the bilayer is integral to the emergence of a unique magnetic profile.  Applying the Herzberg vector analysis, researchers were able to quantify the contributions of valence and conduction bands to the magnetic moment, a finding that suggested a combination of valence and conduction band contributions.  Ultimately, the study of the CrI$_3$ bilayer offers new insights into the complex interplay of magnetic, electronic and band structure properties in 2D magnetic semiconductors, an area of research that is still evolving.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law. Later in its life, it may pass through various rotational states, such as the hydronuclear burning phase, before eventually becoming a white dwarf. Prior to hydronuclear burning, the angular momentum loss it experiences follows the drift time, which is the time it takes for the core's central density to increase by an order of magnitude. According to theory, it is possible for a solar-type star to undergo a magnetic cycle as a byproduct of its rotation-driven convection zone dynamo, but there is limited evidence available to support this theory. Recent computer simulations of a global dynamo model, which takes into account a convective zone that rotates slowly, reveal that a magnetic cycle may not occur if the star's rotational velocity is not rapidly changing and if the area of the convective zone does not expand. Furthermore, the theoretical framework underlying the dynamo quenching mechanism used in the simulation may not be applicable to stars undergoing magnetic cycles. In order to determine if a solar-type star can produce a magnetic cycle, we conducted additional computer simulations of the global dynamo model, employing a more realistic representation of differential rotation that is based on solar observations. Contrary to previous results, our simulations reveal that a quick transition from differential rotation patterns to helical magnetic fields can occur

Deep multimodal learning using K-fan deep Boltzmann machines offers a novel approach to combine multiple input sources. This method can learn a common representation using contrastive divergence and is applied to classification, information retrieval, and other related tasks. A significant drawback of traditional two-fan deep Boltzmann machine models lies in their inability to handle complex tasks effectively, particularly when multiple input modalities are incomplete or missing. We present a K-fan deep model, featuring a K-branch architecture for handling multi-input, multi-output tasks efficiently. Each branch of the model can comprise multiple layers of neural networks. A shared representation is learned in a discriminative manner to tackle multiple tasks. We propose two optimization methods tailored to joint visual restoration and object recognition tasks. Model parameters are initially estimated through maximum joint distribution and then fine-tuned using backpropagation based on the specific task. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the model in utilizing multiple information sources to perform well across various competitive baselines.

The use of model checking has become increasingly essential in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs. Traditional unit and functional tests are insufficient due to the hidden nature of race conditions, which can evade detection by these tests. The McMini model checker, which is based on DPOR, has been expanded with a mechanism that enables the declaration of novel, fundamental thread operations through C code. The mechanism allows end-users to define their own thread activation policies, including the treatment of spurious wake-ups, as well as custom thread creation and management routines. By specifying a run-to-crash strategy, users can identify race-related errors, such as unbounded production of stack frames, null pointer dereferences, and control flow anomalies. By integrating a McMini-verified library, which is based on the McMini model checker, users can determine thread activation periods and detect race conditions on a per-access basis. The model checker's efficiency has been proven in an extension of the standard bakery protocol, which incorporates a drop-counting feature, as well as in the task allocation module of the hard real-time OSEK standard.

The globally predominant messaging app, WhatsApp, boasts a distinct characteristic 
in its closed nature and user-friendly capabilities of transferring multimedia and
large-scale information sharing to groups, which often facilitates the rapid spread 
of anonymous, encrypted messages. However, the direct delivery of messages to user 
phones enabled by WhatsApp, although personal and immediate, can be exploited to 
circulate baseless rumors and fuel misinformation campaigns. Recent elections in 
Brazil and India are notable examples of such abuse, which have led WhatsApp to 
initiate countermeasures like limiting forwarded messages to a single recipient. 
Despite this effort, the success of these measures remains uncertain, particularly 
given the distinct features of each election. To address this knowledge gap, we 
developed a mathematical model based on differential equations to analyze the effect 
of limits on the misinformation epidemic. Our approach transcends the realm of 
WhatsApp, offering a general framework that can be applied to any closed system 
facilitating information dissemination. Our research reveals that the effectiveness 
of limiting the dissemination of information depends heavily on the specific context in 
which it occurs. In cases such as Brazil, this approach may slow down the spread of 
misinformation, whereas in India, the limited timeframe likely allowed the 
misinformation to spread universally. Our methodology can be employed to evaluate the 
potential impact of similar measures in other contexts, such as the recent 
elections in Mexico and Argentina.

We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model, leading to population partition by genetic type. This gives rise to a frequency spectrum, denoted by $A(k,t)$, which counts the number of family groups of size $k$ in the population at time $t$. The frequency spectrum process represents a type of non-Markovian branching process belonging to a class of random-characterized branching processes. This work aims to propose approximation methods that replace this frequency spectrum with simpler quantities and assess the asymptotic error associated with these approximations using central limit theorems. Finally, we apply this model through numerical analysis, focusing particularly on the relationship between one of the proposed approximations and Sabeti's Extended Haplotype Homozygosity measure.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. By selectively amplifying key input characteristics and suppressing irrelevant ones, AReLU enables our system to prioritize artifact-related features. Our proposed system was applied to the logical access task using the ASVSpoof2019 dataset and demonstrated improved performance compared to systems utilizing standard, non-adaptive activation functions.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding.  Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires navigating the constraints on desirable inflationary paths, moduli stabilization to achieve a stable de-Sitter phase, and ensuring the scalars remain heavy compared to the Hubble scale to facilitate single-field inflation.  Additionally, supergravity predicts several non-renormalizable interactions, rendering it an effective field theory that remains valid up to a specific cutoff energy scale, and thus necessitates a re-examination of the scalar potentials and field dynamics to achieve self-consistency at the quantum level.  This thesis, therefore, constructs locally supersymmetric effective field theories of inflation, incorporating recent reforms to the $\mathcal{N}=1$ supergravity formulation that increase the flexibility in the scalar potential space and accommodate KKLT string backgrounds.

Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs rather than the transmission of light. An experiment was conducted and supported by theoretical findings, showing this nonreciprocity through second-order coherence functions of photon pairs created by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. Changing the direction of the pump's propagation leads to significant diminishment in coherence functions while maintaining the transmission.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices.

We demonstrate that the real number line can be divided into a countable number of Borel sets. Specifically, we establish that there exists a sequence of open intervals whose union is the real number line and consists of exactly $2^{\aleph_0}$ distinct intervals, with each interval being a Borel set.

In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. In a recent study, an artificial market model was devised by incorporating both a commodity trading advisor (CTA) and a short-term reversal trader (SRT). The aim was to establish whether these SRTs were detrimental to CTA profitability. Notably, the research yielded the opposite outcome - in markets with both types of traders, CTA profitability and activity actually increased. Consequently, a positive symbiotic relationship between these traders may be more likely than initially assumed.

Identifying the application protocol is a crucial process in network security monitoring that demands a quick and accurate assessment to support detailed inspection. Although pinpointing the application protocol can be challenging, solely relying on static characteristics like port numbers can be insufficient. As a result, advanced and adaptive approaches have been developed for more precise identification. In this research, the mechanisms of dynamic protocol detection in widely used open-source network monitoring tools are examined. Our investigation on HTTP showcases that all evaluated methods are susceptible to evasion tactics, posing significant risks to real-world network surveillance operations. Furthermore, this study reveals that a primary challenge of distinguishing between application protocols remains unresolved in two of the three monitored systems analyzed. To inform operational decisions, this research emphasizes the trade-offs inherent in employing dynamic protocol detection methods.

Electrostatic gating limits the flow of electrons in integrated circuits. Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is difficult to regulate. However, we found that superconducting strips atop thin magnetic films can completely reflect magnons through their magnetic resistance to stray magnetic fields. The significant frequency shifts resulting from this response effectively halt the forward flow of magnons perpendicular to the magnetic field. By positioning two superconducting gates in parallel with the magnetic field, we were able to create a confined magnon system. The added capability to control coherent magnons enables new functionalities in magnonic devices, including reconfigurable logical circuits and stronger connections to other systems of degrees of freedom.

A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, novel classes emerging from unseen data patterns on various devices challenge this methodology as they are not accessible to the central server or fellow users. In response, we suggest a unified system addressing the associated issues during federated learning. Our system is evaluated in two distinct settings - 1) when users conceal the new class labels, and 2) when users disclose this information, whereupon we simulate user data representations by comparing class similarities, and use clustering techniques to differentiate among them. Our system is capable of handling disparities among users' labels and models as well. Our framework is experimentally verified on two prominent applications: voice recognition and urban sound detection. It exhibits a performance increase of 4.0% and 2.0% over the baseline in both scenarios, respectively.

A comprehensive theoretical model is offered in this paper for analyzing high-dimensional entangled systems, specifically the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. Initially, we apply our approach to measure a complete three-photon GHZ state across three dimensions and then extend it to multi-photon systems within higher dimensional settings. In our model, both hyperentanglement of photons and the quantum Fourier transform are employed. The proposed solution will serve as a useful resource for developing high-dimensional quantum computation and communication.

This research paper delves into the problem of uplink cascaded channel estimation in multi-user multiple-input-single-output systems aided by intelligent-reflecting-surfaces operating within the sub-6 GHz frequency range where channel propagation isn't sparse. A high-performance, low-overhead estimation protocol has been developed to minimize reflection power loss without requiring on-off amplitude control. The proposed solution exploits a common structure within the system, significantly reducing pilot transmission overhead by decomposing the complex cascaded channel into separate user-specific and shared variables. The challenge of highly coupled estimation variables is overcome through the use of optimization-based estimation methods utilizing channel covariance. An alternating optimization algorithm has been developed to efficiently solve the resulting non-convex problem. The results show that this approach yields superior performance with minimal overhead compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information.

The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the modular network structure known as the ESBN, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items outside of its initial training scope, similar to how humans can apply learned concepts beyond what they initially learned.

Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming actions, such as accessing a disk or the network. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less storage and processes information faster. A different solution, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as an expansion of the Bloom filter. A modification to this design has also been explored, particularly by Dietzfelbinger and Pagh. Their variation of the Bloomier filter can serve approximate membership queries efficiently, though no comprehensive testing of it exists to date. A different filter was developed, the xor filter, as an implementation of their idea, offering more effective efficiency and speeds. Notably, the developed xor filter can surpass both Bloom and cuckoo filters in performance, all while consuming even less storage space than these solutions. A compact variant of the xor filter was also designed (xor+), resulting in storage needs similar to or smaller than already compressed sequences while providing similar speeds to those seen in Bloom filters.

Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively.

A new approach aims to derive market trend insights from dynamic price equations, specifically those that describe how future prices converge to optimal values, thereby maximizing trading volume per unit of time. This methodology stands out for its inherent ability to select a suitable time frame, which is automatically identified by analyzing past market activity and determining the state of highest trading efficiency. To facilitate trend analysis, both historical and forecasted price data are considered, with past prices represented by lagging values and forecasted prices represented by advancing values.

This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it relies on SMPC operations such as multiplication, addition, and comparison, which omits expensive operations like division and square root. Evaluation on standard image classification datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively blocks malicious submissions and precludes data exposure from the server.

We successfully submitted the winning entry to the NeurIPS 2021 - AWS Deepracer challenge, which required developing a self-driving vehicle model that interacts with its environment through action-reward interactions. The objective was to create an autonomous vehicle model that navigates a simulated track, adapts to real-world settings, and completes a lap at maximum speed while staying on course. The competition was part of The AI Driving Olympics (AI-DO), a series that fosters embodied intelligence advancements in autonomous driving, by benchmarking the progress in applied autonomy. The Deepracer challenge proved to be complex, so we transformed the problem into a two-task model that includes predicting a vehicle's trajectory and achieving a reward by taking actions that lead to a reward. We mitigated the simulation-to-reality gap by using a dataset of real images to normalize our model's expectations of the world's appearance. The combination of a standard transformer and a standard multi-step reinforcement learning approach proved to be effective, leading to the top performance in the competition.

Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincingly authentic deepfakes, which have sparked interest across multiple sectors due to their vast potential applications, despite raising serious societal and security risks. This chapter examines the advancements and difficulties in the production and identification of deepfakes, and also explores the potential solutions to improve the resilience of deepfake detection for a broad range of media, such as real-world images and videos.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring liquid water oceans, provided they do not possess massive H2/He envelopes that would cause them to be excessively hot. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that observable differences exist between the solubility equilibria and thermochemistry of carbon and nitrogen gases in small vs. massive H2 atmospheres, with the requirement for a liquid water ocean and thermal equilibrium being inherently conflicting. Thermochemical recycling of carbon and nitrogen in the massive atmosphere of a temperate exoplanet typically produces CH4 and NH3, while a small atmosphere would contain CO2 and NH3. However, when considering a solubility equilibrium in a liquid water ocean with a massive atmosphere containing CO2 and NH3, the presence of CO2 in the atmosphere is confirmed if NH3 dissolves in the ocean. Conversely, the presence of CH4 in the atmosphere is confirmed if CO2 dissolves in the ocean. We found that the sub-Jovian atmosphere of the temperate exoplanet HAT-P-11b, which has a small size and is thought to be a candidate for a habitable world, exhibits characteristics consistent

Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The model leverages the asymmetry of connections between binary neurons to effectively learn and memorize multiple temporal patterns of binary vectors, an ability similar to that of symmetric Hopfield networks for spatial patterns. Furthermore, our study reveals the model's capability to efficiently acquire sequences of binary images and generate neural spike-train data. Our model adheres to spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) principles, providing a theoretical framework for the systematic design of biological neural networks capable of long-term, robust sequence storage.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text models capable of providing more reliable and robust predictions.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating separate solution branches in parameter-dependent systems and generalizes seamlessly to multi-parameter tracking. To demonstrate the proposed methodology, this research achieves the precise calculation of random equilibrium cycles in the Lorenz system, as well as solution branches and 2-dimensional planes of steady states in the Swift-Hohenberg equation.

The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is challenging due to the inherent limitations of sensors and available resources. Moreover, industrial systems may exhibit multiple failure patterns, and identifying the primary cause is essential. This work aims to develop an adaptive monitoring system capable of handling high-dimensional data in resource-scarce environments where various potential failures may occur. Our proposed solution incorporates the Shiryaev-Roberts method at the failure mode level and employs multi-arm bandit strategies to balance discovery and exploitation. Furthermore, our algorithm's theoretical underpinnings demonstrate its efficacy in isolating the primary failure mode. Through simulations and case studies, we verify that the detection performance of changes and accuracy in isolating the failure mode can be exceptional even in situations where the number of failures or resource constraints are unknown.

We have created a detailed analysis of the origins and development of two disrupted galaxies that merged with the Milky Way's outer layers: the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 systems. Our sophisticated computational model, designed to simulate galaxy growth patterns, is based on exponential infall scenarios and allows for reliable fitting of these patterns. Our analysis led to the discovery of key time frames: 1.01 billion years for GSE to form new stars, while 10 billion years ago, the system experienced initial infall and then maintained its stellar formation for about 1.5 billion years. Conversely, the star-formation times for Wukong/LMS-1 were roughly estimated to be 3.36 billion years. Our model showed strong consistency with other computational methods that fit galaxy growth patterns, our detailed atomic composition data, and the predicted formation patterns for multiple chemical elements. Our unique computational approach, primarily focused on simulating and analyzing isolated galaxy development, allows for accurate fitting of various galaxy growth patterns, demonstrating good agreement with other predictive methods. Our analysis provides insight into how these galaxies' chemical compositions were formed, with variations in that composition across different star-formation episodes. Our detailed time frames for GSE and Wukong/LMS-1 can help solve similar problems for other observed galaxy systems, while our success in fitting these patterns for two galaxy remnants could lead to new understandings of galaxy development. Our model and associated data

Given a profinite group G, an S[[G]]-module is a G-spectrum that fulfills certain criteria, leading to the definition of the homotopy orbit spectrum X_{hG} associated with an S[[G]]-module X. When X's constituents meet specific finiteness criteria, a homotopy orbit spectral sequence arises with an E2-term being the continuous homology of G, taking coefficients from the graded profinite \widehat{\mathbb{Z}}[[G]]-module \pi_*(X). This is demonstrated with an equivalence for certain conditions on G and Z: specifically, (Z[[G]])_{hG} is shown to be equivalent to Z in those scenarios, with supplementary methods for further investigation provided.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy.

The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a semiconductor material crucial for the development of quantum devices. Using a computational model that incorporates machine-learned data and density functional theory, we have studied how varying the bonding configuration at the interface impacts the electronic properties. Across the examined configurations, we observed that the energy levels at the interface in InAs are positioned higher than those in EuS. Furthermore, we discovered novel states that arise from the interaction between the two materials, and are localized at the interface due to charge transfer. The arrangement of atoms at the interface significantly influences both the energy position and distribution of these states. While an induced magnetic effect is evident in InAs, the magnetic moment is relatively weak.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for training. Traditional approaches to speeding up training often involve pre-existing knowledge about the model and require significant adjustments to the network structure. There has been a recent trend in integrating pruning and knowledge distillation techniques to achieve this goal, but previous methods still have limitations in accuracy and efficiency. A new method called ClickTrain addresses these issues by developing a more precise pruning technique that preserves the original model's characteristics, allowing for more effective training acceleration. ClickTrain involves three main stages: architecture-preserving pruning, weight adjusting, and loss function optimization. During the pruning stage, the method analyzes both the pruning pattern and the spatial correlation of the model to determine the best pruning strategy, and then removes redundant weights from the model without altering its original structure. In the weight adjusting stage, the method distributes the remaining weights more efficiently to compensate for the losses incurred from the pruning process. Finally, the method enhances the training efficiency by incorporating knowledge distillation from a larger model to guide the learning process. Experimental results demonstrate that ClickTrain can achieve a speed-up of 2-3 times with minimal accuracy loss, and even improve the accuracy of the model in certain scenarios, all without altering the original network structure. A more robust version of the method, ClickTrain-Plus, is also proposed to integrate knowledge distillation from

This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored to handle subformula propositions that are not necessarily meet or join of other formulas. In the context of this modal logic, we investigate which subformula propositions can act as preconditions for the box operator to validly derive a conclusion. This is analogous to asking which subformula propositions can serve as preconditions for the box operator in first-order modal logic, as per the approach of (Aucher et al., 2013). Our study identifies three distinct categories of subformula propositions, referred to as open, right, and left subformula propositions. By examining the properties of these categories, we demonstrate that open subformula propositions retain the ability to derive conclusions for the box operator, whereas right and left subformula propositions do not possess this capability. Furthermore, we derive a formula that acts as a universal operator for the right subformula propositions and another for the left subformula propositions. In the process, we prove closure properties for these operators and demonstrate their operation through examples. Finally, we investigate the relationship between the distributive full lambek calculus and the subformula modal logic, as well as its relationship with the 2-D topological logic.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Mergers involving neutron stars yield electroweak radiation, providing scientists with the opportunity to explore the nucleosynthesis and the dense matter quark equation of state using the characteristics of the gravitational waves. To take full advantage of the resulting data, researchers must develop enhanced detectors with greater sensitivity to low-frequency signals in the 1-60 Hz range. Resolving the complexities of neutron star gravity, which is poorly understood, requires particular importance. A new approach, Deep Learning Detector, has been created to identify neutron star-black hole mergers within the gravitational wave data, and it outperforms existing models by accurately distinguishing all known neutron star-black hole events with minimal false positives. Furthermore, Deep Learning Detector effectively separates and reconstructs individual gravitational waves from real data, outperforming other machine learning techniques. It achieves this through a deep convolutional neural network design that utilizes the characteristics of the gravitational waves, and by accurately estimating the parameters of the neutron star-black hole events in line with established methods. To take full advantage of the resulting data, future researchers must employ advanced detectors with greater sensitivity to low-frequency signals. A future upgrade to the gravitational wave detectors, anticipated to enhance their sensitivity by approximately 10 orders of magnitude, will particularly benefit the analysis of neutron star-black hole merg

A new discovery has been made of a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star called TOI-5542 approximately every 75 days. TOI-5542 is located approximately 560 light-years away from us, in the direction of the constellation of Bo\"{o}tis. This star, which is about 10 billion years old, has about 0.92 times the mass of our sun and possesses a metal-poor composition. The exoplanet, which has a radius of about 1.26 times the radius of our sun, is most likely a gas giant that has a mass of about 0.53 times the mass of our sun. Based on analysis of the transit data, which showed that the exoplanet has a surface temperature of about 580 K, it is believed to be a mature planet that has reached a stable size. The data also suggested that the exoplanet has a slightly larger radius than expected, which may be the result of it either having a thick atmosphere or having undergone an excessive amount of atmospheric loss. The radial velocity data confirmed the presence of the exoplanet and provided an accurate measurement of its orbital period, which is 75.46 ± 0.03 days, as well as its mass-to-radius ratio, which is 0.31 ± 0.03. The data also suggested that the exoplanet has a slightly elliptical orbit, which has an eccentricity of 0.13

Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs for the development of optimal operational strategies: they are often characterized by an extremely vast number of states and actions, as well as a difficult-to-compute transition matrix. To resolve these challenges, we develop an algorithm that combines policy iteration with subgradient ascent. We show that this approach allows the CMDP to converge to a solution at a rate proportional to $O(\log(T)/\sqrt{T})$, where T represents the number of iterations, provided that a specific condition is met. This method also offers an efficient way to reduce the dimensionality of the CMDP by exploiting its structural properties when applicable. We successfully test the efficacy of our algorithm across a wide range of scenarios, including a high-priority customer service problem and a supply chain management issue, where it yields desirable results.

This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. The approach involves segmenting symbols accurately into over 300 categories. Since many complex mathematical symbols require both horizontal and vertical projection to be split, but certain symbols, like the square root symbol, can't be processed this way. What's more, handwritten mathematical symbols can look very similar, for example, handwritten zero and the Greek letter null. Given the numerous mathematical symbols, over 300 in total, a highly effective classifier capable of recognizing such a wide range of symbols must be developed. Initially, this study addressed the challenge of segmentation by applying the Simple Linear Iterative Clustering method. Results showed that the accuracy of the designed kNN classifier was 84% for the salient features, while 57% and 53% accuracies were achieved with the Histogram of Oriented Gradient (HOG) and Linear Binary Pattern (LBP) methods respectively for the salient features. Also, pixel intensity had an accuracy of 43% for the 66 classes considered. The use of the modified LeNet architecture achieved an accuracy of 90% for 87 classes and the SqueezeNet architecture reached an accuracy of  for 101 classes.

A geometric interpretation is provided for superconformal quantum mechanics based on a hyper-Kahler cone that has a symplectic resolution with equivariant symplectic properties. In this framework, BPS states can be represented as specific cohomology classes in twisted Dolbeault cohomology on the resolved space. The growth rates of BPS state degeneracies, specifically their indices, are connected to Euler characteristic computations in equivariant sheaf cohomology. A notable instance is when considering the Hilbert scheme of points on a 2D plane; this yields an accurate calculation of exponential BPS state degeneracy growth rates as the number of points goes to infinity. The growth characteristics serve as a theoretical prototype for the duality concept we introduced between a 7D black hole and superconformal quantum mechanics.

We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process using numerical methods. Initially, our research reveals that the disparity in epidemic behavior between homogeneous and non-homogeneous networks is largely attributable to the variability in infection rates among individual nodes. Specifically, the average number of infections each node experiences, known as the 'k-out-of-n' rule, differs significantly between the two types of networks, particularly during the transition period where infections are rising. Notably, this discrepancy holds true even when the total connections to each node remain consistent, independent of its position in the network. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the vulnerability of a node, determined by the frequency of its infections, correlates positively with its centrality in the network, indicating that nodes situated in high traffic areas are more likely to be infected.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its practical implementation often results in suboptimal policy outcomes owing to the limitations inherent in the actor-critic architecture. To address these shortcomings, our approach integrates the actor-critic model with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for a hybrid framework termed the Hamiltonian Policy. In doing so, our novel method has numerous benefits, primarily in reducing the gap between the approximated posterior and optimal policy distribution. Furthermore, our approach optimizes exploration within action spaces by targeting areas with higher expected returns. To achieve this, a new leapfrog operator has been developed for simulating Hamiltonian dynamics. Consequently, our approach has shown significant policy improvements, with empirical evidence indicating better policy evaluations and target policy convergence in challenging Monte Carlo policy search tasks. Moreover, our results indicate that the Hamiltonian Policy is capable of achieving superior performance on difficult continuous control tasks.

It's widely recognized that any prime number $p$ greater than or equal to $5$ can be represented as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. We will refer to the number $k$ that produces a given prime $p$ as the $\textbf{generator}$ of that prime. Pairs of twin primes have the unique characteristic of sharing a $\textbf{common generator}$. As a result, searching for these twin primes at the level of their respective generators makes practical sense. This paper introduces a novel strategy for verifying the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ by utilizing a sieving approach to extract all twin primes at their corresponding generator levels. In the context of $\omega_{p_n}$-numbers, $x$, we are referring to numbers that satisfy the condition that $6x-1$ and $6x+1$ are relatively prime to the prime $p_n$. We can demonstrate the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ by utilizing the average gap distance $\bar{\delta}(p_n)$ between the $\omega_{p_n}$-numbers in an indirect manner.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in real-time, the proposed system incorporates a sonar sensor filter to process data from a single or multiple sensors and simulate human spatial awareness. By utilizing this information, a layered controller module can determine the robot's position and orientate itself within the environment. This study presents an in-depth analysis of the simulated and experimental outcomes, confirming the system's ability to function in real-time and accurately calculate the robot's position, even when operating a single sensor in a narrow environment or multiple sensors in a larger space.

Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that can be spectroscopically analyzed, exhibits an irregular orbit. Our analysis focuses on Nereid's spectral characterization utilizing its reflectance spectrum between 0.8-2.4 $\mu m$, particularly in the unexplored 0.8-1.4 $\mu m$ range, as we attempt to identify the spectral absorption features that correspond to its icy composition. Our findings indicate the presence of crystalline water ice, coinciding with existing observations. Nonetheless, using simple models consisting of intimate water ice mixtures, we fail to attain a comprehensive match of absorption bands, especially considering the spectral features at 1.5 $\mu m$. This could be resolved by supposing that Nereid's surface is composed of micro-crystalline water ice, as well as other minor constituents. Additionally, discovering spectral features at 0.8-0.9 $\mu m$ was found to be challenging, though this may be attributed to limitations of our spectral resolution. Our findings suggest the presence of highly tholinated materials, such as those found on Triton, however this requires further investigation. Finally, combining bi-static information, along with existing analysis, we find the bound on the albedo of Nereid's surface to be in the range of 3-50%.

Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of order $n \geq 2$, consisting of elements from the finite field $F(q)$ of order $q \geq 2$. Additionally, let $V_{2n}(q)$ be the free left module of its counterpart ${^2T_n(q)}$. Studies have proven that over the projective line based on $T_n(q)$, we find subplanes isomorphic to $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$* and $V_{2n}(q)$, where *denotes the dual ring operation. This paper continues these investigations by exploring the existence of affine and projective planes linked with projective lines based on $T_n(q)$. It is shown that a projective plane based on $T_2(q)$ is isomorphic to the grid plane if and only if its dual is based on $F_2(q)$. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence of its existence to that of an affine plane based on $F_2(q) \times F_2(q)$.

In a 1983 paper in J. Symbolic Logic, Pawlikowski demonstrated that under specific conditions regarding Cohen and random reals, certain model properties can be inferred for extensions of those models. This is proven through a novel application of Tukey-order with models, expanding upon an existing concept introduced by Vojtáš in 1991. By leveraging this notion, it can be shown that certain model properties can imply each other, thereby establishing key theorems related to random and Cohen reals within the context of Tukey-order.

A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness significantly depends on this parameter's proper choice. Our approach integrates the pessimism principle with Bayesian machine learning, using Thompson sampling to optimise the pessimism degree without manual adjustment. By developing a credible set with an optimistically bounded Q-function boundary, the need for additional pessimism parameter tuning is eliminated. Our generalizable theoretical findings demonstrate both the reliability of our approach in finding the optimal policy and the efficiency of our approach in finding a policy that performs nearly as well as the best possible. Additionally, simulations and a real-world analysis are examined to illustrate our approach.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be defined by the relationship to Wakamatsu tilting bimodules, with specific cases yielding known results with respect to tilting modules, almost complete tilting modules, and tilting sets. When restricting to dualities involving tilting modules, this relationship can express various mathematical concepts in terms of tilting, such as equivalences, contractions, extensions, and compositions. Additionally, by imposing certain conditions on tilting modules, this duality can be seen as a combination of multiple tilting modules, yielding new duality concepts and confirming previously proposed definitions. The proof of a previously proposed duality concept also follows directly from the relationship. The purpose of this paper is to establish and prove this relationship, providing a new perspective on tilting modules and duality, with potential implications for homological invariants.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. Despite their different sizes, both arrangements are linked to a common 8D lattice with 240 fundamental vectors, tied to the E8 Lie algebra. An exploration of this setup's properties employs many comparisons to the Witting configuration's attributes.

In a flat band superconductor, bosonic modes can freely propagate whereas unpaired electrons are fixed in place. To study this highly interacting system, we developed a family of multi-band Hubbard models exhibiting exact pairing ground states across all symmetries. Through analytical computations, we discovered that many-body excitations are governed by an effective single-particle Hamiltonian based on the non-interacting wave functions of the system, which now features a dense spectrum of quasi-particle states. We found that both the superconducting gap and the density of states exhibit $log$-scale independence on the chemical potential, and that a collective mode exists at approximately 4K in the superconducting state. We also observed experimentally that pairing tendencies are weakened by disorder, whereas the superconducting nature is entirely robust against magnetic impurities. Furthermore, we discovered a range of non-Fermi liquid behaviors in the system, characterized by the exponent $\sim \pm i \ln(1/\delta)$, where $\delta$ is the correlation length, and the pairing angle $\theta$.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables.
